articles.title: Si eres fan de Apple, iOS 27 tiene un detalle escondido que te va a encantar: así se activa
articles.text:
Hace mucho que Apple no recurre a los huevos de Pascua para firmar sus sistemas operativos y darle a los usuarios un motivo más para hurgar en sus ajustes. Esto acaba de cambiar con iOS 27: la californiana ha querido volver a lo de antaño (y nunca mejor dicho) con un easter egg que no muchos entenderán, pero que transmite muchísima nostalgia para quienes lleven muchos años en el ecosistema. Y cuando decimos muchos, es muchos: la referencia data de 1984 y muestra un detalle actualizado del Mac original.
Encontrar el nuevo huevo de Pascua es bastante sencillo, aunque primero debes actualizar tu iPhone a iOS 27. Cuando lo tengas, debes ir a Ajustes, abrir el apartado de 'Apariencia' y después pulsar sobre 'Liquid Glass'. Luego baja hasta que encuentres la primera imagen de muestra que dice "Bienvenido al Apple Park" y sigue pasando todas las imágenes una por una.
Cuando llegues a la última imagen, sigue deslizando hasta que en la barra de búsqueda aparezca la palabra "¡Moof!" y la imagen cambie. Este es Clarus, el perro-vaca que en el pasado se convirtió en un icono de la compañía muy popular entre los desarrolladores, pero que pasó un poco desapercibido para el público general.
Durante muchos años fue la mascota oficial de la compañía de manera interna, y todo comenzó en 1984 cuando el glifo se creó como parte del primer sistema operativo Macintosh con interfaz gráfica. Era una imagen de mapa de bits que ahora se ve muy anticuada, pero Apple la ha actualizado con iOS 27 para despertar a los más nostálgicos.
Durante muchos años, Clarus se utilizó para identificar la forma correcta de imprimir una imagen o un documento a través de los Mac, dejando claro cuál era la posición correcta para que el texto no se viese volteado. Algo que ahora todos los PCs hacen de forma automática, pero que en la década de los 80 no era algo tan sencillo.
Apple vuelve a despertar la nostalgia con iOS 27
Es solo un pequeño guiño, pero para muchos de los fans de la compañía supone algo más. Con la llegada de John Ternus, muchas cosas han cambiado en Apple, convirtiéndose en pocos días en una compañía más similar a lo que era en la época de Jobs.
La dinámica más centrada en el hardware y el desarrollo que está implementado Ternus se ha dejado ver en este easter egg de Clarus, dejando una sensación bastante buena para todos los que echan de menos cómo se comportaba la compañía con los pequeños detalles hace algunos años.
Apple llevaba tiempo sin recurrir a los huevos de Pascua, y ahora Clarus, sin servir para nada, nos deja un toque retro en iOS 27 que puedes ver cuando no sepas qué hacer con tu iPhone.

articles.title: Anthropic warnt vor KI-Biowaffen – doch Forscher widersprechen
articles.text:
KI als Bedrohung? Wissenschaftler kritisieren Anthropic-Report zu Biowaffen
Am 12. September 2026 hatte Anthropic-CEO Dario Amodei öffentlichkeitswirksam dazu aufgerufen, dass die KI-Branche ihre Entwicklung drosseln müsse. Als einen Grund brachte Amodei die jüngsten Sicherheitsfälle um KI-Agenten ins Spiel, die eigenmächtig aus eigentlich als sicher geltenden Testumgebungen entkamen und andere Websites hackten.
Amodei-Warnung: Forscher bezweifeln Gefahr
Nur wenige Tage, bevor der Anthropic-Chef vor einem dadurch drohenden Kontrollverlust warnte, machte sein Unternehmen mehrere Fälle öffentlich, bei denen Nutzer:innen die KI angeblich für Anfragen rund um die Entwicklung von Biowaffen verwendet haben sollen. Entsprechende Versuche habe Anthropic unterbunden. Doch unabhängige Forscher:innen zeigen sich skeptisch ob der tatsächlichen Bedrohung.
Konkret soll sich eine der von Anthropic blockierten Anfragen etwa darum gedreht haben, wie sich Vogelgrippe auf Säugetiere übertragen lasse. Eine andere Person habe Hilfe dabei erhalten wollen, einen Antrag auf Förderung für die Forschung an einem Virus zu verfassen. Dabei sei es darum gegangen, die Übertragbarkeit von Erregern zu erhöhen.
KI für Biowaffen? Anthropic fordert Verbot
Insgesamt veröffentlichte Anthropic fünf solcher Fälle. Doch das seien nur einige potenziell bedrohliche Aktivitäten, die das Unternehmen auf seiner Plattform entdeckt habe. Für CEO Amodei ein Grund für die Forderung, die Möglichkeit, per KI Biowaffen zu entwickeln, auf internationaler Ebene zu verbieten.
Doch einige Forscher:innen widersprechen der von Anthropic aufgebauten Bedrohungskulisse. So erklärte etwa der Evolutionsbiologe Kristian Andersen, dass die meisten, wenn nicht alle der in dem Report beschriebenen Versuche einfach Grundlagenforschung seien. Ein KI-Unternehmen wie Anthropic könne wohl kaum entscheiden, welche Art von Forschung vorangetrieben und welche gefährlich und damit beendet werden müsse, so Andersen gegenüber Science News.
Forschung zur Entwicklung von Gegenmitteln
Schließlich könnten die Anfragen wissenschaftlicher Forschung dienen, die sich mit der Entwicklung von Gegenmitteln beschäftigt. Das räumte übrigens auch Anthropic selbst ein. Der Biosicherheitsexperte Gregory Koblentz von der George Mason University stützt die Argumentation Andersens. Die von Anthropic vorgebrachten Fälle drehten sich ausnahmslos um Krankheitserreger, die in verschiedenen Teilen der Welt endemisch und damit eine Bedrohung für die öffentliche Gesundheit darstellten. Ihre Erforschung, so Koblentz, sei daher nicht verdächtig.
Auch einen weiteren Punkt, den Anthropic als Beleg für seine Warnung heranzog, kritisierten Andersen und Koblentz. Die KI-Firma hatte berichtet, dass einige Forscher:innen per VPN versucht hätten, für ihre Länder geltende Verbote zu umgehen. Doch das, so Koblentz, sei doch kaum überraschend. So sei Anthropics Claude in China verboten. Warum sollten chinesische Forscher:innen nicht versuchen, irgendwie dennoch an entsprechende Informationen zu kommen.
Uplift-Versuch gefährlicher als Forschungen
Was bei der möglichen Entwicklung von Biowaffen für die befragten Forscher wirklich gefährlich wäre, seien Menschen ohne wissenschaftliches Grundwissen, die versuchten, sich per Claude entsprechend weiterzubilden. Und die mit einem solchen „Uplift“ dann etwa gefährliche Krankheitserreger erzeugen könnten. Doch bei den von Anthropic vorgebrachten Fällen scheint es sich, so die Forscher, um etablierte Wissenschaftler:innen zu handeln, die Claude lediglich zur Unterstützung für ihre Arbeit heranziehen wollten.

articles.title: Microsoft confirms KB5002914 Excel update breaks copy and paste
articles.text:
Microsoft has confirmed that copy and paste may silently fail for some Excel users after installing the September 2026 KB5002914 security update.
This follows a wave of customer reports on Reddit and the Microsoft Q&A forums that the KB5002914 Office security update is breaking copy-and-paste, autofill, and formula dragging in Excel.
"Although users try to paste content, the source remains selected and the destination is unmodified," Microsoft said in an updated support document confirming these issues.
"When this issue occurs, users receive no indication of the failure, such as a beep or error message. Microsoft is researching the issue and will post more information in this article when the information becomes available."
In a separate service alert seen by BleepingComputer, Microsoft said the issues affect Microsoft Excel 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016, and are caused by a code regression.
"A code regression contained within a recent service update is causing impact," it said. "Our development and validation of the individual fixes targeting each of the impacted versions is ongoing, and we'll provide an estimated timeline for resolution as one becomes available."
While Microsoft is still working to resolve this bug, affected Excel users have reported that uninstalling KB5002914 restores copy-and-paste functionality on impacted systems.
To do that, open a new Command Prompt window with the "Run as administrator" option and run one of the following commands (depending on your Office version):
Office 2016:
"C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\OFFICE16\Oarpmany.exe" /removereleaseinpatch "{90160000-0012-0000-1000-0000000FF1CE}" "{27882596-A8ED-4382-9C71-6CD2DD19F732}" "1033" "0"
Office 2019:
"C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\OfficeC2RClient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.10417.20197
Office 2021 & 2024:
"C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\OfficeC2RClient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20326.20132
Microsoft released the KB5002914 security update last week as part of its September 2026 Patch Tuesday to patch a long list of remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities.
In July, Microsoft also fixed an issue that was preventing third-party applications from launching Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Access, and other Microsoft Office apps or opening documents on up-to-date Windows systems.
One month earlier, Microsoft addressed another bug that blocked Office for the web users from opening Excel and PowerPoint files, and another that blocked Windows 365 users from downloading and installing the Office suite.
On Monday, it also released emergency out-of-band updates to resolve Remote Desktop Services failures caused by the September 2026 security updates, along with Hyper-V and USB audio problems on some Windows versions.

articles.title: Bolt is giving developers 50x more compute. But there's a catch.
articles.text:
Bolt is giving developers 50x more compute. But there’s a catch.
Bolt.new, StackBlitz’s browser-based AI development platform, is testing a new trade with developers: more coding-model usage in exchange for training data.
The company launched Forge on Monday, a research preview for individual Pro subscribers that offers up to 50 times more usage of open weight coding models through October 14. Developers who use Forge must opt in to sharing anonymized versions of their sessions for model training, including prompts, source code and the fix traces it creates as developers work through problems, in addition to their conversations with the coding agent.
The sessions will be used in a project with Arcee AI to help train a trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The first training run is scheduled to begin in October, with Bolt saying the resulting model weights will eventually be released publicly.
Forge makes that development activity part of the exchange, with developers getting more compute while Bolt and Arcee get data from real coding sessions.
Why Coding Trajectories Matter
Public repositories contain enormous amounts of source code, but they mostly show the end result. A coding session can fill in the gaps left by failed attempts and revisions along the way. The record of what worked (and what did not) is useful as the coding agents take on longer jobs.
Working across a codebase means finding the right files, coordinating changes, and recovering when something breaks. That gets harder when agents inherit code written by other agents, which isn’t always easy for the next one to understand or modify.
SpaceXAI showed one version of this approach last month when it trained Grok 4.6 on agent failure traces — the missteps, retries, and corrections that other labs typically discard. Bolt is making a similar bet but sourcing the data from developer sessions rather than synthetic runs.
Arcee has been working on the same underlying problem. In a blog post about NAC, its open-source agent harness, the company said software engineering tasks can stretch across tens of thousands of tokens as agents read code, edit files, run tests, and debug failures.
How Bolt Gets to 50X More Usage
Coding agents can burn through large numbers of tokens on even a single complex task, so a 50-fold increase in usage is a truly significant offer.
Forge changes the underlying setup by running open weight models on Bolt’s own infrastructure. The agent currently uses GLM 5.3 Flash and GLM 5.3, with Kimi K3 and DeepSeek v4 Pro available as experimental options.
Bolt’s WebContainers technology, built by parent company StackBlitz, gives it another cost advantage by running projects in an isolated environment inside the user’s browser rather than on Bolt’s servers.
Forge applies a similar approach to the models, using open weights on reserved hardware while developer sessions help train future versions, giving Bolt more control over costs and reducing its reliance on proprietary APIs.
That push toward self-hosted models is showing up elsewhere in the industry. Nvidia’s $12.9 billion bid for Hugging Face is arguably the same bet at a very different scale.
Coding agents can burn through large numbers of tokens on even a single complex task, so a 50-fold increase in usage is a truly significant offer.
Forge Scores 91% of Bolt’s Top Model
Forge’s open models scored 92.2 on the company’s internal Bolt Build Index, compared with 101.0 for its top paid model, putting them at about 91% of the top score. That’s only a measure of performance inside Bolt, so the 91% figure doesn’t tell us how those models compare more broadly.
But if Bolt can run more of its coding workloads on its own models instead of paying for proprietary APIs, it has more control over costs and usage, while the Forge sessions help train whatever comes next.
What Developers Are Giving Up
Forge requires an explicit opt-in, with a consent screen appearing each time a developer switches into the workspace. Standard and Max sessions aren’t included, and Teams and Enterprise accounts can’t participate.
Bolt says it anonymizes sessions before they leave its infrastructure, removing secrets, sensitive data, and personal information, and it tests the process against seeded data. Arcee receives the resulting data under a signed processing agreement.
Developers can stop sharing new sessions by leaving Forge, but Bolt says anything already used for training will remain in the models.
The 50× surge ends October 14, though Bolt says Forge itself will stick around as an open-model testing ground once the preview wraps up.

articles.title: Avec sa nouvelle offre SFR Fibre sobriété, l'opérateur tente de se la jouer écolo
articles.text:
Avec sa nouvelle offre SFR Fibre sobriété, l'opérateur tente de se la jouer écolo
SFR a la fibre écolo *badum tss*
Qu'il s'agisse d'une véritable volonté écologique ou de greenwashing pour redorer son image avant la fin, SFR vient de lancer une nouvelle offre fibre. Elle s'appelle SFR fibre sobriété et a quelques arguments à faire valoir auprès des personnes qui souhaitent réduire leur impact sur la planète.
Alors que son rachat par les autres opérateurs ne devrait pas être bouclé avant fin 2027, SFR ne va pas bien. Entre la fuite de nombreux clients et les difficultés logiques pour en recruter de nouveaux, le début de la fin a commencé pour l'opérateur au carré rouge, dont la réputation n'était déjà pas au mieux avant même cette massive opération. Qu'à cela ne tienne, voici venir en ce mardi 15 septembre 2026 une nouvelle offre fibre, peut-être bien la dernière.
SFR fibre sobriété, l'Internet avec une touche écolo
Dévoilée dans le cadre des Semaines du Développement Durable, cette offre s'intitule SFR fibre sobriété. Son objectif : proposer un accès Internet qui va à l'essentiel, basé sur une box reconditionnée, et doté d'un petit bonus pour les plus écolos.
Facturée à un tarif fixe de 27,99 €/mois, avec un engagement de 12 mois, SFR fibre sobriété rappelle à première vue d'autres offres d'opérateurs concurrents côté tarif et offre. Il est en effet question d'un accès à Internet allant jusqu'à 1 Gb/s en montant et en descendant, avec appels illimités vers les fixes en France et plus de 100 destinations. Pour la première fois chez SFR, pas de décodeur supplémentaire dédié à la télévision donc, mais un service TV avec 160 chaînes incluses via l'application SFR TV (disponible sur TV connectées, ordinateurs et appareils mobiles).
Attention, des frais d'ouverture de service de 49 € sont également de la partie, tandis qu'il est possible de demander à SFR un remboursement des frais de résiliation et d'engagement de son ancien opérateur jusqu'à 100 €.
Là où l'offre tente de se démarquer, c'est sur son côté écolo. Tout d'abord, la box proposée, la SFR Box 7 en WiFi 5, est reconditionnée. Ensuite, chaque mois SFR fait un don d'un euro à A Tree for You, une association qui finance des projets pour "un développement humain en harmonie avec l'environnement", façon Ecosia. Il est notamment question de replanter des haies du bocage normand par des agriculteurs locaux.
Suffisant pour convaincre de nouveaux clients de tenter la fin de l'aventure SFR ? Pas sûr, d'autant que les solutions de Free, Sosh (Orange) ou encore B&You (Bouygues Telecom) sans décodeur proposent généralement des box plus performantes (mais neuves), des débits supérieurs ou des prix inférieurs. L'écologie a un prix.

articles.title: Près de quatre heures contre Elon Musk : le documentaire choc qui détruit le mythe autour du milliardaire
articles.text:
La Mostra de Venise a projeté le 8 septembre, hors compétition, l’un des films les plus attendus de sa sélection : Musk, portrait-fleuve de l’homme le plus riche du monde signé Alex Gibney. Le documentariste américain s’est fait une spécialité des empires qui s’effondrent, d’Enron à Elizabeth Holmes. Son nouveau sujet, lui, règne toujours sur Tesla, SpaceX et X, ce qui donne à l’exercice un parfum inédit de procès en direct.
Un portrait de bonimenteur, pièces à l’appui
La thèse du film tient en une idée : derrière le génie autoproclamé se cacherait un bonimenteur prêt à tromper, manipuler et affabuler pour parvenir à ses fins. Pour l’étayer, Gibney aligne les témoins de premier rang : Martin Eberhard, cofondateur évincé de Tesla, Justine Musk, première épouse du milliardaire, la journaliste Kara Swisher ou encore Geoffrey Hinton, figure tutélaire de l’intelligence artificielle. Eberhard raconte qu’on lui aurait promis que personne ne pourrait jamais lui retirer son statut de fondateur de Tesla ; l’histoire, procès à l’appui, a démontré le contraire.
Le passage le plus dommageable concerne la conduite autonome, le dispositif qui occupe les législateurs des pays européens (France comprise) depuis le début de l’année. Une déposition d’ingénieur exhumée par le film affirme qu’une célèbre vidéo promotionnelle de Tesla avait été mise en scène, la voiture ayant percuté une barrière pendant le tournage. Le documentaire relie par ailleurs le logiciel maison à 65 morts sur les routes. Une ex-compagne de Musk y raconte aussi avoir reçu des SMS évoquant des milliers de « lasers dans l’espace », puis un message où l’intéressé se dirait « un peu défoncé ». Le film s’attarde enfin sur le passage éclair de Musk à la tête du DOGE, la commission chargée de tailler dans les dépenses fédérales américaines. Une ancienne responsable de l’aide internationale y évalue à 14 millions le nombre de morts évitables qui découleraient du démantèlement de l’agence USAID. L’équipe juridique du milliardaire dénonce un film mensonger, conteste notamment la séquence des lasers et agite la menace de poursuites en diffamation ; Gibney, lui, assume l’intégralité de son montage.
Un clone de Musk généré par IA, la fausse bonne idée du film ?
Musk ayant refusé de s’asseoir devant la caméra, Gibney a comblé le vide avec un choix qui divise : un double de Musk généré par intelligence artificielle, chargé d’incarner sa parole publique. La critique, pourtant conquise (100 % d’avis positifs recensés après Venise), tique précisément sur ce procédé, jugé malaisant dans un film qui reproche à son sujet de brouiller la frontière entre réel et fiction. Utiliser l’arme de l’adversaire pour mieux le confondre, le pari est audacieux ; il rappelle surtout que plus personne n’échappe à son propre deepfake, pas même celui qui possède Grok.
Côté calendrier, la sortie américaine en salles a été avancée au 9 octobre, avant une diffusion en streaming ; l’international est confié à un grand studio, mais aucune date française n’est encore annoncée. Les distributeurs hexagonaux savent pourtant compter : quatre heures de démolition méthodique du patron de Tesla, voilà un produit d’appel dont l’actualité ne se dément jamais très longtemps.
En attendant une date de ce côté-ci de l’Atlantique, le film dispose déjà du meilleur argument publicitaire qui soit : la fureur de son sujet.

articles.title: iOS 27 donne aux parents de nouveaux outils pour protéger leurs enfants, voici lesquels
articles.text:
Avec la sortie d’iOS 27, iPadOS 27 et macOS 27, Apple déploie une nouvelle suite d’outils de contrôle parental. Configuration simplifiée, autorisation de navigation, protection étendue contre la violence : voici ce qui change concrètement pour les parents.
Apple avait consacré dix minutes entières à ce sujet lors de la WWDC en juin, du jamais-vu pour une thématique de contrôle parental. La promesse se concrétise désormais : depuis le 14 septembre, ces nouveautés sont disponibles sur l’ensemble des appareils mis à jour. Voici les possibilités qui s’offrent désormais aux parents pour accompagner l’usage numérique de leurs enfants.
Une configuration simplifiée et une navigation mieux encadrée
Créer un compte Enfant reste la première étape indispensable, une démarche même devenue obligatoire en France lors de la première mise en service d’un appareil. Avec iOS 27 et iPadOS 27, l’Assistant réglages propose désormais des sélections prédéfinies d’apps pour faciliter cette configuration, souvent perçue comme fastidieuse. Un premier niveau, baptisé « apps essentielles », se limite à Téléphone, FaceTime, Messages, Plans, Boussole et Réglages. Un second niveau, plus permissif, ajoute Photos, Appareil photo, Notes et Fichiers. Il reste bien sûr possible d’autoriser n’importe quelle autre application au cas par cas, dès le départ ou plus tard.
Autre nouveauté très attendue : la fonction Demander à Naviguer. Cette fonctionnalité permet aux parents d’exiger une approbation avant que leurs enfants n’accèdent à un nouveau site web dans Safari. Concrètement, une demande est envoyée au parent directement dans Messages, qui peut l’approuver ou la refuser, sur le même principe que le système « Demander à acheter » déjà utilisé pour les téléchargements d’applications. Si votre enfant veut se rendre sur un site web particulier pour ses études, ou pour se divertir, il devra avoir votre accord.
La sécurité des communications s’élargit également. Jusqu’ici centrée sur la détection de nudité dans les photos et vidéos échangées, elle bloque désormais aussi les images et vidéos sanglantes ou violentes dans les contenus partagés, y compris lors d’appels FaceTime en direct. Les visuels sont floutés dès réception et l’enfant est invité à consulter ses parents.
Des plages horaires plus souples, à condition que tout le monde soit à jour
Le système Temps d’écran connaît lui aussi une refonte en profondeur avec les Limites de temps. Plutôt que d’imposer une restriction rigide application par application, les parents définissent désormais des budgets de temps par catégorie entière, comme les réseaux sociaux, le divertissement ou les jeux. Apple fournit des conseils de spécialistes adaptés à l’âge de l’enfant, élaborés avec l’aide d’experts en santé et sécurité en ligne, dont l’American Academy of Pediatrics, dont le Family Media Plan sert désormais de référence pour adapter ces recommandations. Ces repères restent un simple point de départ, ajustable à tout moment selon les besoins de chaque famille. L’interface de Temps d’écran, qui était devenue une usine à gaz assez difficile à pratiquer, a par ailleurs été repensée pour offrir une vue d’ensemble de l’utilisation en un coup d’œil, avec des commandes accessibles d’un seul toucher pour ajuster l’accès dans l’instant.
Un point mérite toutefois une attention particulière avant de se réjouir trop vite : pour bénéficier de la mise à jour Temps d’écran, tous les appareils d’un même groupe de Partage familial doivent être mis à jour vers iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27 et visionOS 27. Un iPhone à jour ne suffit donc pas si un iPad plus ancien de la famille, hérité par exemple d'un parent, reste bloqué sur une version antérieure faute de compatibilité.
Avant de configurer ces nouvelles protections, mieux vaut donc vérifier que tous les appareils utilisés par l’enfant, y compris les plus anciens, sont bien éligibles à la mise à jour. La disponibilité des fonctionnalités peut par ailleurs varier selon les zones géographiques, les langues et les modèles. Pour plus d’infos, Apple a d’ailleurs publié une page complète à l’attention des parents pour paramétrer dans le détail ces nouvelles fonctions.

articles.title: Piraté, le compte officiel de HBO Max a servi à diffuser des malwares sur Reddit
articles.text:
Cinq vagues de publicités sponsorisées ont déferlé sur Reddit en l’espace de 48 heures, mettant en danger tous les fans de HBO Max qui les ont croisées sur la plateforme.
Au total, 108 annonces malveillantes ont été diffusées depuis u/hbomax, le compte officiel et vérifié de la plateforme de streaming.
L’alerte a été donnée par un utilisateur, qui a repéré l’une de ces publicités. L’affaire a ensuite été documentée conjointement par les chercheurs d’ADAMnetworks et de HudsonRock, qui ont publié leurs conclusions le 13 septembre 2026.
Selon leur enquête, les annonces faisaient la promotion d’une application HBO Max native pour macOS (qui n’existe pourtant pas) et redirigeaient vers un faux site imitant l’identité visuelle officielle du service.
Le piège ClickFix
Plutôt que d’exploiter une faille technique, l’attaque misait sur la manipulation.
En cliquant sur le bouton de téléchargement du faux site, les internautes tombaient sur une fenêtre ClickFix : une simple invite leur demandant de copier une commande, d’ouvrir le Terminal (sur Mac) ou un équivalent Windows, puis de la coller et de l’exécuter.
En procédant ainsi, c’est la victime elle-même qui lance le programme malveillant, contournant du même coup une bonne partie des protections censées bloquer un téléchargement suspect.
L’objectif final : pousser la victime à télécharger un infostealer pour voler identifiants, données de navigateur, messages et informations de portefeuilles de cryptomonnaie.
Sur Windows, une partie du trafic malveillant était même déguisée en connexions Facebook pour échapper à la détection.
Publicités suspendues, ampleur encore floue
Une fois informée de la situation, Reddit a suspendu les publicités liées au compte compromis. Warner Bros., propriétaire de HBO Max, a été contacté pour réagir à cet incident, sans réponse à ce jour.
Ni Reddit ni les chercheurs n’ont communiqué de détails concernant le nombre d’utilisateurs ayant réellement cliqué sur ces publicités et exécuté la commande piégée.

articles.title: Vilnius-based EnforceShield raises €1.7 million Seed round to fight AI-powered IP abuse with autonomous enforcement | EU-Startups
articles.text:
EnforceShield, a Vilnius-based LegalTech startup that shields businesses from intellectual property violations, has raised a €1.7 million Seed round for its attorney-built, autonomous intellectual property (IP) enforcement platform.
The round was led by Vendep Capital, with participation from FIRSTPICK VC, and the capital will be used to expand the platform into more sophisticated workflows and broader IP lifecycle management.
Artis Bisers, Investment Manager at Vendep Capital, said, “AI has made turning service businesses into software into a massive opportunity, and legal services are ripe for this shift. Finding counterfeits was never the hard part for brands. The value lies in everything that happens after discovery, and EnforceShield handles the entire process in a single system rather than stopping at detection.
“Rytis worked on this problem himself for years before building the company, which is precisely the expertise needed to automate it properly. This team has shown it can turn that knowledge into product at genuine speed. We are delighted to be backing them as they extend that automation to every channel where brands are being copied.”
Founded in 2024 by Rytis Rudzinskas, a practising attorney with a background in running digital IP enforcement operations, EnforceShield is an autonomous IP enforcement platform for enterprise IP holders. Its systems continuously detect, analyse, and execute enforcement actions against IP rights violators at a scale human-only teams can no longer handle.
The company claims that it’s the AI-powered answer to AI-powered IP abuse. Rudzinskas mentions that he has seen firsthand that throwing an ever-increasing number of lawyers and analysts at IP enforcement would never solve its scaling problems. With IP abusers increasingly relying on AI, Rudzinskas realised IP enforcement had to respond in kind.
The Lithuanian startup notes that it runs as a SaaS solution for continuous, autonomous IP enforcement, executing the complete workflow from cross-platform detection through legal analysis, validation, takedown execution, monitoring, and escalation, rather than simply identifying potential infringements for a human team to handle.
It further notes that Validation applies jurisdictionally appropriate legal logic to each case before the system executes platform-specific takedowns and monitors for recurring violations. This logic encompasses evaluating factors such as evidence packs, original brand IP portfolio, applicable laws, likelihood of confusion, unauthorised use, platform context, and enforcement success criteria.
EnforceShield opines that attorneys and analysts shouldn’t be tasked with the repetitive operational work of routine infringement cases; therefore, it is designed to execute it autonomously from the outset.
The platform’s AI agents make case-level enforcement decisions using its built-in, jurisdiction-dependent legal and platform-specific decision logic. This enables its “human-at-the-end” model, where analysts and attorneys only approve system outcomes and handle flagged exceptions or complex escalations.
Rudzinskas, CEO and founder of EnforceShield, said, “When I founded this company, I felt we were already operating on borrowed time. Generative AI had made IP abuse a booming business, but enforcement was still largely a human-scale operation. Enterprises didn’t need more lawyers or even a software co-pilot. They needed tech that’s able to think like a lawyer and pilot itself through enforcement workflows.
“We started by reworking the legal operational workflows I’ve spent years building and operating manually and encoded that expertise into a system that can run autonomously. EnforceShield is now freeing human teams from a glut of repetitive work they’ll never manage manually, and developing the most sophisticated software that can perform the operational enforcement function itself and at scale.”
According to the startup, this design decouples enforcement volume from headcount: enterprises can handle dramatically higher case volumes without scaling their legal or brand-protection teams in proportion.
It’s also what makes same-day onboarding possible. EnforceShield asks for minimal upfront data, ingests it directly, and returns results, often surfacing infringements clients didn’t even notice.
The company is headquartered in Lithuania with a US subsidiary in Tennessee. It plans to use this capital to grow the overall technical and product capacity needed to automate the next layer of the IP enforcement process. The next phase of development will extend EnforceShield agents beyond standardised takedowns to manage escalation, repeat offenders, and more complex enforcement pathways. 
The platform already operates globally, and the funding will also support commercial expansion in the US, which already accounts for up to 80% of EnforceShield’s sales pipeline.

articles.title: Gates Foundation pledges $1 billion to drive AI equality globally
articles.text:
Gates Foundation pledges $1 billion to drive AI equality globally
AI access gets a $1 billion boost. The Gates Foundation plans to support AI in education, healthcare and agriculture, with a focus on underserved communities.
The Gates Foundation has pledged at least $1 billion to expand access to AI over two years. The funding will focus on communities that have often been left behind by new technologies.
The announcement followed the launch of the foundation’s 10th annual Goalkeepers Report. It says AI could help bridge gaps in healthcare, education and livelihoods if governments, tech companies and other stakeholders take the right steps.
The 2026 report, Make This Matter: AI, Equity, and the Choice We Can’t Delay, says the opportunity to influence who benefits from AI is narrowing as the technology develops rapidly.
Making AI useful beyond English
The report identifies three areas that need attention. The first is language. More than 90% of the data used to train early large language models came from English-language sources, according to the foundation. This leaves many communities underrepresented in the data used to develop AI tools.
The foundation is calling for AI systems that work across the languages people actually speak, rather than concentrating capabilities around a small number of dominant languages.
The second priority is context. AI tools need data and expertise from the communities where they will be used, while countries and communities should have a say in how their data is managed and protected.
The third is access and skills. Doctors, farmers, teachers and developers need opportunities to understand, evaluate and adapt AI tools for their own needs. Affordable access to the technology will also require investment from governments and philanthropy, alongside action from technology companies.
Where the $1 billion will go
The Gates Foundation plans to distribute the funding across four priority areas. Education will receive 40% of the commitment, supporting AI tutoring designed to personalise student learning and teaching tools for classrooms in the US and other countries.
Another 40% will go towards healthcare, including diagnostics, clinical decision-making support for frontline health workers, maternal and newborn care tools, and the discovery of drugs and vaccines.
Agriculture will receive 10%, including efforts to provide smallholder farmers with AI-generated advice tailored to their soil, weather and crop conditions.
The remaining 10% will support the digital foundations needed for equitable AI, which includes datasets in languages that current AI tools do not sufficiently understand.
Gates calls for deliberate action
Bill Gates, chair of the Gates Foundation, said AI could repeat an existing problem in which people with the greatest needs have the least influence over where innovation and investment are directed.
“AI presents the same challenge, only at much greater speed,” Gates writes in the report.
He argues that leaving development entirely to market forces could result in the most capable tools being built first for users and institutions that can pay the most, rather than those who could benefit the most.
The foundation’s funding will therefore support partners already working to close gaps in AI access and ensure that tools reflect the knowledge and priorities of the communities they serve.
“We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident,” Bill Gates writes.
The foundation is also calling on governments, technology companies and others to contribute funding, expertise and influence to make AI more useful, accessible and affordable.
The report’s central argument is straightforward: AI’s impact is not predetermined. How widely its benefits are shared will depend on the choices being made now.

articles.title: Plus besoin de tout trimballer : cette sacoche française à 90 € intègre son propre antivol — Frandroid
articles.text:
Overade a déjà marqué le secteur du vélo électrique avec ses casques, le pliant Plixi et le complet Life qui nous avait épatés lors de notre essai. La marque française propose aussi d’autres produits comme la sacoche vélo Loxi, qui possède une caractéristique unique en son genre.
Une version 15 litres qui s’accroche au porte-bagages
L’Overade Loxi est un produit 2-en-1, à la fois sacoche et antivol. Avec son cadenas à 4 chiffres et son câble de 12 mm de diamètre, elle sécurise le contenu. On peut ainsi laisser son casque, ses gants ou quelques affaires sans risquer le vol.
Overade ne survend pas pour autant son idée. La marque reconnaît que le câble de 12 mm et le tissu anti-coupure ne garantissent pas une protection à 100 % contre le vol, et déconseille même de compter sur la Loxi pour attacher le vélo lui-même, en rappelant que ce n’est pas un antivol à proprement parler mais un sac doté d’un cadenas pour le maintenir en place. En clair, la Loxi décourage le vol d’opportunité sans remplacer un antivol en U pour immobiliser sa monture sur la durée.
La firme parisienne superpose en fait deux couches : une bâche PVC à l’extérieur, qui assure l’imperméabilité, et une doublure en tissu anti-coupure de niveau 5 (fibre de verre, polyester et polyéthylène UHMWPE), censée résister à une lame de cutter – Overade l’annonce même 40 % plus résistante que le kevlar. Avec sa fermeture zip doublée d’une seconde à enroulement façon rolltop, la sacoche résiste aussi à la pluie.
La Loxi existe aussi dans une grande taille de 15 litres, dont le câble de 53 cm, plus long, peut se boucler autour d’un point fixe. Elle se fixe sur des porte-bagages arrière jusqu’à 16 mm de diamètre, avec un dos rigide et une fixation inférieure pour rester stable en roulant.
La version 9 litres, avec une sangle pour s’attacher au cadre, est aussi au catalogue, tout comme la plus petite de 4 litres, apparue en 2018.
Question encombrement, la version 15 litres pèse 820 grammes et la 9 litres 660 grammes. Assez léger, donc, pour la laisser à demeure sur le porte-bagages, même vide, sans vraiment alourdir le vélo.
Une sacoche-antivol vélo abordable
La sacoche vélo 2-en-1 avec antivol Overade Loxi est disponible sur le site officiel ainsi que chez les revendeurs. Le prix varie en fonction de la version, que voici :
- Loxi 9 litres : 90 €
- Loxi 15 litres : 109 €

articles.title: Hoy en Lidl, la cafetera retro en tonos pastel que cuesta 59,99 euros y con la que preparar café como el del bar, pero en casa
articles.text:
Si estás buscando darle un toque de estilo a tu cocina sin gastar una fortuna ni renunciar a un buen espresso, Lidl tiene uno de esos chollos que suelen durar poco en stock. La cadena alemana vuelve a poner a la venta su cafetera express Silvercrest SEM 1100 E1, un modelo de brazo manual con estética vintage en tono pastel, que puedes conseguir en su tienda online por 59,99 euros.

articles.title: The picture in her head: How this blind creator teaches AI to be her eyes
articles.text: Omolara Daniel sits at her laptop, describing the logo she wants in painstaking detail. She tells an AI tool what she wants the design to look like, waits for it to generate the image, then asks the tool to describe what it has produced. If the description does not match the picture in her mind, she prompts it again. When she is satisfied, she sends the design to a friend for a final check. Daniel is blind. She cannot see the logo she has just created. “I just enjoy doing this. It is becoming something that makes me want to give AI a big thumbs up every day,” she says. Finding ways to work independently The designs are only one part of the business Daniel runs largely on her own. From her home, she runs Cura Heritage Foods Ltd, formerly Tosaf Foods, where she produces natural spices, cereals, and snacks. She handles production, sales, and marketing herself. Omolara wears a headset during a meeting at a conference table. Image Source: Omolara Daniel, a visually-impaired Nigerian entrepreneur. “I have the sole responsibility for my business currently,” she says. “I don’t have any staff. I manage both production, sales and even marketing.” Her production process begins at the market, where she sources the ingredients she needs. Back home, she cleans and detoxifies them before putting them through a dehydrator. She measures the ingredients with a talking scale, blends them in her milling machine, and packages the finished products herself. She has gradually adapted each stage of the process so she can work with less assistance. When she started the business, she used a regular digital scale and depended on sighted people to tell her what she had measured. She eventually bought a talking scale that announces the weight aloud. “With or without anybody, I can single-handedly manage my production process,” she says. The next challenge was creating the visual content she needed to market the business. Seeing through AI For Daniel, visual content was once an area where independence stopped. Much of the work depended on details she could not see, so she initially relied on other people to create or review it. Omolara Daniel at the Kaduna State Government House in 2020. Image Source: Omolara Daniel/Facebook. “The first logo I did for my business was designed for me by a graphic designer,” she says. “[At the] time, I didn’t have knowledge of how to use AI to do graphics.” As AI tools became more accessible, Daniel began to wonder whether she could use them herself. She was already interested in technology and did not want her disability to determine what she could learn. “As a blind person, you don’t want to be behind,” she says. “As technology is advancing, you also want to advance.” In 2025, while interning in the IT department of the telecoms company MTN Nigeria, she says she was exposed to more technology, including AI. The experience deepened her interest, and she decided to learn more about it, paying for training rather than waiting to pick up the skills for free. She learned to work with several AI tools, including Claude, Gemini, Veo 3, Google Flow, and Microsoft Clipchamp, using them at different stages of her creative work. But she soon realised that getting the result she wanted depended on how clearly she could communicate her idea to the technology. “Before you can prompt AI, you yourself need to know what you want,” she says. “The mental notes of exactly how you want something to come out. You need to know it.” From ideas to visuals For graphics, Daniel starts with the picture in her mind and gives AI chatbots such as Claude and Gemini what she describes as a vivid account of what she wants. She uses them to refine her ideas and develop detailed instructions before taking those prompts to other tools. If she has a preferred colour, she specifies it. If she does not, she asks the AI to suggest a suitable combination. “AI is just like garbage in, garbage out,” she says. “What you want, it’s your prompting at the end of the day.” For video projects, the process involves several tools. After refining her prompts in Claude, she moves to Veo 3, where she generates individual scenes rather than attempting to create an entire video at once. She then assembles the scenes in Microsoft Clipchamp. If a scene does not convey the idea she has in mind, she generates it again and keeps refining it. Once she is satisfied, she sends the work to a friend, sibling or, in some cases, a client for a final check. The reviewer may identify something that needs to be changed, and Daniel returns to the AI tool to make the adjustment before sharing the work again. The arrangement sometimes comes with an additional cost. The people helping her review the work may need to download the files or watch the videos, which can consume data. “Sometimes I have to buy data for them because they also have to download, and some of them will complain, ah, my data,” she says. Omolara Daniel works on her laptop while wearing a headset at her workstation. Image Source: Omolara Daniel. The skill has also become a small side hustle. Daniel occasionally creates logos, flyers and videos for other businesses. Some clients find her through referrals after seeing work she has produced for someone else. “I have somebody who reached out to me this week because they saw a video that I did for someone,” she says. “I really liked the video. Please, I also want to do for my business.” The limits of the tools The finished graphics can make the process look simpler than it is. Daniel says she can usually complete a logo in about an hour, but videos take longer because she creates them scene by scene and relies on others to verify each one. “They are very stressful to an extent because I have to make and remake,” she says. “Most times I have to make them scene by scene to start with, and then share with people who vet it and let me know that, ‘Oh, this one, the AI didn’t do it well.’” Some videos have eight or 10 scenes, she says. If one fails to convey the message she intended, she generates it again. And because the people who help her review the work are not always immediately available, a task that might otherwise take minutes can stretch much longer. Clients can add another layer of difficulty. One flyer once kept her at her laptop for about five hours as a client requested repeated changes. Daniel eventually abandoned the job after the AI repeatedly failed to produce what the client wanted. Then there is accessibility. Before settling on the tools she now uses, Daniel tried several others, paying for subscriptions simply to find out whether they worked with her screen reader. “Many of them are not that accessible, to be honest,” she says. “And many of them, when you hear about them, oh, this one can do this, this one, then you go and check it out, and you see that the interface is not screen reader friendly.” CapCut was one of the tools she abandoned for that reason. “Accessibility-wise, a laptop is easier because I can easily flow. Just like a sighted person will flow,” she says. “When I try to do things on my phone, it slows me down, and I feel like it stresses me mentally.” Still, the assistance Daniel needs has changed. She is no longer handing the creative work entirely to someone else. She can develop an idea, turn it into detailed prompts, generate the work, and refine it herself, bringing in other people only to verify the visual details she cannot see. For Daniel, that shift is about more than creating content for her natural foods business or earning an occasional fee from other businesses. It is about having another skill she can carry into whatever comes next. “The most important benefit of having this skill is personal,” she says. “It is not even for the business side of it, or I want to make money from it. It is the fact that I can do this on my own, and if I walk into any working environment where the skill is needed, I will fit in.” True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Texas Utility CenterPoint Energy Confirms Breach After Hacker Leaks Data
articles.text:
Texas utility CenterPoint Energy confirmed on Monday that a threat actor has obtained customers’ personal information. The disclosure comes just days after a hacker claimed to have stolen millions of records.
CenterPoint Energy is a Houston-based public utility that delivers electricity and natural gas to roughly 7 million customers across Indiana, Minnesota, Ohio, and Texas.
The company told the SEC that it has launched an investigation after becoming aware of someone claiming to have obtained customer information.
“While the investigation remains ongoing, the Company has determined that an unauthorized third party obtained personal information relating to a portion of the Company’s customers through one of the Company’s external facing systems,” it said in the SEC filing.
The utility noted that the cybersecurity incident has not impacted the delivery of electric and gas services and it does not believe that the data breach will have a material impact.
The company’s disclosure comes after a hacker leaked data allegedly stolen from its systems. The claims were made on a popular cybercrime forum on September 12.
The hacker allegedly obtained nearly 7.5 million user records, threatening that “next time we won’t simply pull data, we’ll start attacking the main infrastructure.”
The threat actor has made available for download a 2.5 GB archive file allegedly containing data stolen from CenterPoint Energy. SecurityWeek cannot confirm the validity of the data and it’s not uncommon for hackers to make false or exaggerated claims.
This is not the first time a hacker has claimed to have stolen CenterPoint Energy data. In 2024, it was one of several energy companies targeted by an access broker named AntiBrok3rs.
A few months later, a different hacker claimed to have obtained the company’s data. In both cases, the stolen data was believed to have come from the Cl0p ransomware group’s 2023 MOVEit campaign. Analysts believed at the time that the CenterPoint Energy data originated from a third party rather than directly from the company’s systems.
Related: 240,000 Hit by Data Breach at Japan’s Digital Agency

articles.title: Amazon Linux 2027 Enters Public Preview with SELinux Enforcing by Default
articles.text:
AWS has released Amazon Linux 2027 in public preview, built on the AL2023 baseline and shipping with SELinux in enforcing mode by default. That default is the change most likely to create work for teams planning a migration, and the announcement does not say when AL2023 support ends or when AL2027 reaches general availability.
AL2027 runs on kernel 7.1 or later, uses AWS-LC for cryptographic operations, and adds accelerator drivers including AWS Neuron support for machine learning workloads. AWS positions it for web applications, databases, containerized microservices, AI and ML workloads, and large-scale infrastructure.
The kernel version is not settled. Benjamin Herrenschmidt, a principal engineer at AWS, noted in a LinkedIn discussion of the release that the kernel will be updated until it reaches LTS, so 7.1 is a starting point rather than what AL2027 ships with at general availability.
SELinux enforcing is the operational difference. AL2023 ships SELinux in permissive mode, where policy violations are logged rather than blocked. Under enforcing mode, they are blocked. Applications that run on AL2023 because SELinux only complained about their behavior will fail on AL2027 unless their file contexts, ports, and access patterns match policy. Validating that is the preview's most useful purpose.
The first question in the community response was about migration rather than features. On Reddit, a commenter asked whether there would be an in-place migration path from AL2023 to AL2027. The question drew more upvotes than any other comment in the thread and no answer from AWS.
Another user replied that cloud-native usage replaces hosts rather than upgrading them in place. The original commenter accepted the principle and named the exception:
I understand, but even in a world of cattle, unfortunately there are always going to be things stuck as pets.
A third suggested EC2 root volume replacement as a partial route for instances that keep no state on the root volume, which covers some cases rather than the general problem.
The gap between release cadence and adoption showed up in the same thread. One commenter noted that he was still working to get teams in his organization onto AL2023.
Preview coverage is broad but incomplete. AMIs are available through the console in all commercial regions in x86-64 and ARM variants, and container base images are on the Amazon ECR Public Gallery. On-premises images are not yet available. A member of the Amazon Linux team, whose GitHub account appears on the project issue tracker, wrote in the same Reddit thread that the team found a last-minute issue and would release those images soon.
The choice of Amazon Linux over other RHEL-derived distributions came up in both threads. One commenter on r/aws said he did not trust IBM to avoid forcing Rocky, Alma or Oracle to re-engineer how they work again, a reference to Red Hat's source availability changes. On r/linux, another placed Amazon Linux against a different comparison:
No, it's more like Oracle Linux. Owned by a terrible company, yes, but it is completely open source and genuinely is no-strings-attached, unlike Oracle Java with its restrictive license. It's not an attempt at vendor lock-in nor is it a proprietary platform.
He added that there is little reason to use it because it is a redistribution of something available elsewhere, which is the counterargument to AWS's cloud-optimization case.
For teams evaluating the preview, the practical work is testing against SELinux enforcing rather than benchmarking the kernel. AWS publishes a full list of changes relative to AL2023 in the AL2027 documentation, and accepts feedback through the AL2027 GitHub repository.

articles.title: Cost Per Frame: Nvidia Stops Offering Good Value GPUs to Gamers
articles.text:
GPU pricing is all sorts of messed up, something we recently covered in depth in a separate article. But one aspect we didn't spend much time on was how this affects the current competitive landscape between Nvidia, AMD, and Intel.
We know GPU pricing has gone up considerably across the board, and generally speaking, GeForce GPUs have risen more than Radeon and Arc graphics cards. But where does that leave the key battles across different price points and regions?
Granted, with the market in its current state, we're not sure how many of you will actually be interested in updated cost-per-frame charts based on current GPU prices to then use this data to go out and purchase a graphics card, but at the very least, it's an interesting look at where things stand after substantial price changes over the past month.
The pricing data here is identical to what we showed two weeks ago, gathered across the same 10 countries using the same methodology and showing the lowest price for in-stock models. Performance data comes from our latest testing, so the margins between cards should be similar to our latest big benchmark reviews looking at 50+ games. Those tests include a mixture of rasterized and ray-traced titles.
MSRP
First, a brief refresher on what the market should look like with every card selling at MSRP. This is roughly where things stood a year ago, before the huge upward pricing trend began.
The best-value GPUs on the market were typically Intel's Arc B580 series, which undercut competing models with aggressively low prices at or below $250. The Radeon RX 9060 XT series wasn't far behind, especially if you wanted higher performance and more VRAM for a modest increase in price.
In the mid to upper end of the market, the Radeon RX 9070 XT and RX 9070 tended to make the most sense. At its proper $600 price, the 9070 XT delivered a 12% lower cost per frame than the RTX 5070, and nearly 20% lower cost per frame than the RTX 5070 Ti.
The RTX 5050 made absolutely no sense at its price given its low performance, while the RX 9070 GRE, which arrived later at the same $550 price as the RX 9070, also would have made little sense if every GPU were selling at MSRP.
United States
Here's where things actually stand in the US market right now. The first thing you might notice is that we've omitted the RTX 5090 from this chart entirely. At $5,000, we simply don't consider it a gaming GPU anymore. That's workstation pricing, and naturally, its cost per frame for gaming is atrocious.
For this analysis, we want the focus to remain on genuine gaming products. If the RTX 5090 falls back to something more sensible, it can regain its status as a gaming GPU and return to these charts. For now, it doesn't make the cut, just as the RTX Pro 6000 doesn't make the cut.
At the entry level, the best-value GPU right now is technically the Arc B570, which offers a slim 8% lower cost per frame than the RX 9060 XT 8GB. The Arc B580 is very similar to the 9060 XT 8GB by this metric, though it comes with more VRAM at 12GB versus 8GB, a precious commodity these days. The only other card sitting below $400 is the RX 5050, which offers significantly worse value because it's much slower.
The next tier up has the RX 9060 XT 16GB and the RTX 5060 at similar prices. Not only does the 9060 XT 16GB have double the VRAM, it's also considerably faster, making the Radeon GPU 17% cheaper per frame. Neither model is ideally priced given they're supposed to sit in the $300 to $350 range, but at around $450, the Radeon card seems like a much better buy.
With price increases affecting the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and RTX 5070, Nvidia is leaving the $600 price tier pretty much unopposed these days. The RX 9070 GRE and RX 9070 offer similar value in terms of cost per frame in this range, although the 9070 is slightly ahead and comes with more VRAM, 16GB versus 12GB.
The closest GeForce GPU to $600 is the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, a comparatively poor purchase.
The RX 9070 XT offers similarly strong value and dominates the upper price tiers in terms of cost per frame. Around this price, we also have the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and RTX 5070, neither of which is competitive.
The 9070 XT is 24% cheaper per frame than the RTX 5070 and a massive 37% cheaper per frame than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. Not even a feature like DLSS can compensate for a discrepancy in raw performance that large. The RTX 5070 Ti doesn't fare much better, with the 9070 XT currently offering a 27% lower cost per frame.
Australia
In Australia, the overall shape of the market is similar to the United States, although some specific matchups shift around. In the US, for example, the RTX 5060 competes with the RX 9060 XT 16GB on price, whereas in Australia, the GeForce model lines up more closely with the 9060 XT 8GB.
The Radeon card is still 8% cheaper per frame, but this does make GeForce significantly more competitive at the lower end of the GPU market. That said, over the past few days we've noticed both models becoming more expensive than the prices recorded a week ago.
At around $700, the RX 9060 XT 16GB competes against the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, and this is a pretty clear win for the Radeon card. Not only is it 17% cheaper per frame, it also offers double the VRAM, which makes a considerable difference in modern games.
At around $900, we have the RX 9070 and RX 9070 GRE competing against the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. So this isn't quite the 9070 XT versus 5060 Ti 16GB battle we see in the US, but it's still a very poor position for GeForce. The 5060 Ti 16GB is the second-worst-value GPU in the Australian market, with the RX 9070 offering a 39% lower cost per frame.
At $1,100, we also have the RX 9070 XT versus RTX 5070 battle, where the Radeon GPU delivers a 15% lower cost per frame while also offering more VRAM. As in the US, the RTX 5070 Ti isn't competitive here, costing more than $400 extra.
United Kingdom
In the UK, Intel's Arc GPUs aren't as competitive on value, which pushes the RX 9070 into the top spot on the cost-per-frame chart. This model costs £550, compared with £600 for both the RTX 5070 and RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, resulting in a 17% and 37% lower cost per frame, respectively.
The RX 9070 XT is also good value for a little more money, though not quite as strong as the RX 9070.
If you're after an entry-level GPU, the RX 9060 XT 8GB doesn't make much sense in the UK. It's priced at roughly the same level as the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB while offering worse value than both that card and the RTX 5060.
None of these models are particularly compelling given they all have just 8GB of VRAM, but it's also a tough ask to spend another £100 on the RX 9060 XT 16GB. That model isn't amazing value either and costs 33% more. So the UK market looks reasonably healthy if you're shopping for a higher-tier GPU, but underwhelming for budget buyers.
The premium GeForce offerings aren't in a great position right now, which, somewhat ironically, makes the RTX 5080 look relatively good. It costs roughly twice as much as an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB but also delivers nearly twice the performance, leaving it just 8% more expensive per frame.
At MSRP, the RTX 5080 carries a healthy high-end tax, costing 25% more per frame than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. That gap has shrunk dramatically as memory-driven price inflation has pushed up the cost of lower-tier GeForce models.
Canada
In Canada, Arc GPUs are in a reasonable position relative to other low-end options. The B580, for example, is 9% cheaper per frame than the RX 9060 XT 8GB. Around the same price you'll also find the RTX 5060, which offers decent value, and the RTX 5050, which is much worse.
We haven't seen quite as much price inflation for the RTX 5060 in Canada as we have in the US, so GeForce remains reasonably competitive at this end of the market.
The next tier up brings us to the RX 9060 XT 16GB, which delivers similar cost-per-frame value to the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB. We'd comfortably recommend the Radeon model, however, thanks to its much larger VRAM capacity.
From there, there's a huge price gap to the next GeForce options, with the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB at $920 and the RTX 5070 at $1,080. Here, the RX 9070 XT is 25% cheaper per frame than the RTX 5070 and 33% cheaper than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, leaving AMD firmly ahead in this price range.
As in the UK, the RX 9070 GRE is reasonably priced, but it isn't enough of a standout relative to the other 9070 models to compensate for its lower memory capacity.
Germany
Heading back to Europe, the Arc B570 is the clear cost-per-frame leader in Germany, followed by a large group of mostly Radeon GPUs. Despite appearing much higher on the chart, the RX 9060 XT 8GB offers only an 8% lower cost per frame than the RTX 5060 and RTX 5060 Ti 8GB. That's decent value, but hardly a runaway win for AMD.
The clear entry-level standout is the RX 9060 XT 16GB. It's priced similarly to the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, offers slightly better cost-per-frame value, and comes with double the VRAM. We'd happily spend the extra €65 over the 8GB 9060 XT to get this variant.
Once we reach the €600 mark, we find the RX 9070 and RX 9070 GRE from AMD alongside the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, which is actually more expensive than both Radeon models. Comparing the RX 9070 with the 5060 Ti 16GB, the Radeon GPU is 34% cheaper per frame, making it the obvious choice.
The RX 9070 is also slightly better value than the 9070 XT, and we'd choose it over the GRE as well thanks to its additional VRAM, despite both cards landing in a similar position on the value chart.
The RX 9070 XT's nearest competitor is the RTX 5070, with both priced at around €720. This leaves the Radeon model 18% cheaper per frame, while it also delivers a 33% lower cost per frame than the RTX 5070 Ti.
Interestingly, there isn't a huge difference in value between the RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5080 in Germany. It's getting to the point where anyone considering a 5070 Ti might be better off paying the relatively small premium and stepping up to the 5080 instead.
Netherlands
In the Netherlands, we're not seeing a huge difference compared with Germany. The RTX 5070 is slightly better value here, narrowing the gap between it and the RX 9070 XT, but the RX 9070 is still significantly better value than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, despite both models selling at the same price.
The main difference is probably the RX 9060 XT 16GB, which is actually better value per frame than the 8GB model in this market, largely because the 8GB version is far too expensive.
India
The Indian market is quite unusual at the moment. GPU buyers there are getting absolutely hammered on GeForce pricing. As you can see in the chart, there's a clean split, with all five Radeon models at the top and Nvidia's GPUs below them.
There are some pretty wild discrepancies here. The RX 9070 XT is 29% cheaper per frame than the RTX 5070, 41% cheaper than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, and 42% cheaper than the RTX 5070 Ti.
The closest battles are at the lower end of the market. The RX 9060 XT 8GB is just 10% cheaper per frame than the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, but given the pricing of the RX 9060 XT 16GB, that's the model we'd choose. It costs the same as the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB and only 10% more than an RTX 5060, while offering 16GB of VRAM.
The RTX 5050, as in many other regions, remains a truly abysmal choice.
Philippines
In the Philippines, it's much the same story. The RX 9070 XT is 29% cheaper per frame than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, although it's just 11% cheaper than the RTX 5070, one of the smaller margins we've seen between those two products.
The RTX 5060 offers reasonable value at the lower end of the market, with an overall price that's 20% lower than the RX 9060 XT 16GB. But again, if you can afford it, we think the 16GB Radeon model is the better choice given its similar cost per frame and much larger VRAM capacity.
Poland
Poland looks very similar to the other European markets, even if the currency is different. Pretty much everything we said about GPU value in Germany applies here, and the general ordering of cards is nearly identical between the two regions.
The Arc B570 isn't quite as much of a standout in Poland, but Intel's Arc models still top the chart by a slim margin.
Brazil
Lastly, we have Brazil, where a few interesting things are happening. The RTX 5060 tops the chart for the first time, offering 5 to 8% better value than the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB and RX 9060 XT 8GB.
That's a reasonable position for a mainstream model, especially given that the RX 9060 XT 16GB isn't particularly good value in this region. The RTX 5060 is 16% cheaper per frame.
There are still sizable gaps between Radeon and GeForce in the upper parts of the market. The RX 9070 XT is 15% cheaper per frame than the RTX 5070 and 26% cheaper than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. There's an even larger margin to the RTX 5070 Ti, while the RTX 5080 is especially poor value here, particularly compared with its relative cost per frame in some European markets.
What We Learned: Nvidia Leaves the Door Wide Open for AMD
That's our look at graphics card value based on cost-per-frame data across a range of regions. While there are some outliers depending on the specific country, the overall trends are remarkably consistent: GeForce GPUs have increased in price more than Radeon GPUs over the past month, making AMD's lineup considerably more competitive.
The bad news for Nvidia, and good news for AMD, is that Radeon now dominates the higher-end segments of the market. The RX 9070 XT should be competing in roughly the same price range as the RTX 5070, while carrying around a 20% price discount relative to the RTX 5070 Ti. Instead, the 9070 XT is now more than 30% cheaper than the 5070 Ti in many cases, creating some enormous discrepancies in value.
Depending on the region, either the RX 9070 XT or RX 9070 also tends to offer better value than the RTX 5070, and massively better value than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, which has somehow ended up in a similar price tier. The 5060 Ti 16GB should not be anywhere near this segment, but the ongoing memory crisis has pushed it to ridiculously high prices.
The mainstream and entry-level markets have been somewhat more resilient, and this is where the battle between Nvidia and AMD remains more competitive.
In many regions, the RX 9060 XT 16GB occupies a strong position simply because of its higher VRAM capacity, even when it doesn't offer a clear advantage in cost per frame.
There are some notable exceptions, however. In certain markets, the 9060 XT isn't particularly good value, and cards such as the RTX 5060 can make more sense.
If we focus strictly on the cheapest models, mostly 8GB cards along with a few Arc GPUs, competition is at its strongest, and often there isn't much separating the GeForce and Radeon options.
Generally, we'd recommend spending more to get the RX 9060 XT 16GB because it's more capable today and should offer better longevity. But if you're trying to spend as little as possible, the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT 8GB are often competitive with one another.
The main model to avoid is the RTX 5050, which offers atrocious value in every single region we examined.
It's also possible that the value picture we're seeing today won't last very long. We expect Radeon GPUs to become more expensive throughout the remainder of 2026, which could weaken their position relative to GeForce. But we've also been hearing that GeForce pricing has further to climb, suggesting Nvidia's current prices may not have reached their ceiling either.
If both brands continue getting more expensive, the relative margins we're seeing today could remain largely intact. Exactly how that plays out is difficult to predict, but it's something we'll continue watching closely.
Ultimately, this cost-per-frame analysis is mostly an exercise in seeing how competitive each GPU lineup is under today's rather ugly market conditions. None of these GPUs are particularly well priced right now, and as things stand, we don't recommend buying a new graphics card unless you absolutely need one.
If you do need to buy, this data should help identify the least painful options. For everyone else, sticking with the GPU you've already got seems like the much better move right now.

articles.title: Scaling AI Infrastructure With PCIe Switches And Retimers
articles.text:
Build configurable PCIe subsystems spanning local expansion, shared resource domains, and longer-reach topologies.
Artificial intelligence is changing more than the amount of compute inside the data center: it is changing how architects think about where resources live, how they connect, and how efficiently they are used.
AI training, inference, high-performance computing, analytics, and cloud services all demand greater data movement and more accelerators. However, these workloads do not share one ideal architecture. Some need resources located as close together as possible, while others benefit from expanding across servers. Still, others can gain efficiency by sharing expensive devices through a common fabric.
The result is not a wholesale move from traditional servers to one universal disaggregated design. It is a hybrid future built from scale-up, scale-out, and selective disaggregation with PCI Express (PCIe) providing a familiar foundation for connecting critical resources.
Fig. 1: Different workloads create different requirements for bandwidth, latency, locality, and utilization.
Scale-up brings more compute and acceleration into a tightly coupled system. This approach can deliver excellent locality and low latency, making it attractive for demanding AI workloads. However, it eventually encounters practical limits in processor lanes, enclosure space, power, cooling, and the number of devices a host can support.
Scale-out expands performance across multiple servers using Ethernet or InfiniBand. It is essential for distributed computing and cluster growth but introduces network latency and requires software that can coordinate workloads and data across nodes.
Disaggregation separates selected resources such as GPUs, NVMe storage, or SmartNICs/DPUs from fixed server ownership, and makes them available through a shared fabric. This can improve utilization and allow compute and endpoints to scale independently. However, sharing also introduces new considerations around contention, isolation, management, and latency.
To decision makers, the distinction matters because each model changes system performance, capital efficiency, deployment flexibility, and operational complexity. The right question is therefore not, “which architecture wins?” but rather “which resources should stay local, which should scale across servers, and which are valuable enough to share?”
PCIe is already the standard attachment technology for CPUs, GPUs, accelerators, SmartNICs/DPUs, and NVMe storage. Its established hardware and software ecosystem makes it a practical starting point for next-generation infrastructure.
PCIe 7.0 doubles the raw per-lane data rate of PCIe 6.x to 128 GT/s and delivers up to 512 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth in a x16 configuration. That bandwidth supports growing accelerator counts and increasing data-intensive platforms while preserving backward compatibility with the broader PCIe ecosystem. Not only is PCIe 7.0 a major force in data centers today, but PCIe 5.0 and PCIe 6.x also remain major building blocks for today’s infrastructures.
Of course, higher speed does not automatically create a scalable system. As signaling rates rise, channel loss, reflections, crosstalk, noise, and jitter become more difficult to manage. Architects also need a way to connect more endpoints than native host ports alone can accommodate. This is where PCIe switches and retimers take on complementary roles.
Fig. 2: PCIe raw transfer rate per lane has doubled with each generation, reaching 128 GT/s with PCIe 7.0.
A PCIe switch expands connectivity by receiving transactions, identifying their destination, and forwarding them between upstream and downstream ports. It enables higher fan-out, more flexible topologies, and peer-to-peer paths among connected devices.
But port count and peak speed tell only part of the story. In real systems, GPUs, storage, and control traffic may compete for bandwidth at the same time. Arbitration, buffering, credit management, oversubscription policy, and avoidance of head-of-line blocking all affect usable performance.
Switch topology matters as well. Every additional hop adds latency and creates another potential point of contention. A well-designed fabric must provide the required connectivity while minimizing unnecessary stages on latency-sensitive paths.
For silicon teams, configurability is especially valuable. Support for different port widths, upstream-port options, endpoint counts, and traffic patterns can allow one switch architecture to serve multiple products and deployment models.
As resources move farther from the host – across longer board traces, connectors, cables, expansion chassis, or rack-oriented designs – the electrical channel becomes more challenging. A PCIe retimer recovers the clock and data, terminates one electrical segment, and retransmits a clean signal into the next.
Retimers can restore channel margin and give architects greater physical flexibility, but they do not make reach unlimited. Each retimed segment must still be engineered and validated. Designers must account for latency, power, thermals, equalization, diagnostics, and interoperability across hosts, endpoints, PHYs, connectors, cables, and firmware.
The goal is not to add as many retimers as possible. It is to use the minimum number required to meet reach and signal-integrity objectives with acceptable system tradeoffs.
Fig. 3: Switches expand and direct connectivity; retimers extend reliable electrical reach to shared resource pools.
In simple terms, a switch decides where traffic goes and a retimer helps it arrive reliably. Rambus PCIe Switch and Retimer Controller IPs provide complementary building blocks for ASIC and FPGA implementations. The Switch IP addresses connectivity, fan-out, and traffic management while the Retimer IP addresses signal regeneration and reach. Together, they can help design teams build configurable PCIe subsystems spanning local expansion, shared resource domains, and longer-reach topologies.
The strongest evaluation begins with a representative workload and topology, not a feature checklist. Teams should define required bandwidth and latency, expected fan-in and fan-out, oversubscription, traffic mix, channel loss, power, manageability, and interoperability targets. They can then judge switch and retimer capabilities against measurable technical and business outcomes.
AI infrastructure will continue to evolve through a mix of tightly coupled systems, larger clusters, and selectively shared resources. PCIe 7.0, along with PCIe 6.x and 5.0 supply important bandwidth headroom, while switches provide scale and retimers provide reach. Used together, they give architects practical tools to connect more resources, place them more flexibly, and extract greater value from next-generation infrastructure.
