articles.title: Cómo se verían Los Saja Boys de Las Guerreras K-pop en el universo de Tom y Jerry
articles.text:
Recrear a Los Saja Boys, los antagonistas de Las Guerreras K-pop, dentro de una escena de caricatura inspirada en el humor de Tom y Jerry requiere combinar referencias visuales sin copiar personajes ni diseños protegidos.
La creación puede realizarse en Gemini, la herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) de Google que permite generar imágenes a partir de indicaciones escritas y sumar archivos de referencia.
PUBLICIDAD
El método requiere cinco pasos: seleccionar las imágenes, cargarlas al chat, elaborar el prompt, descargar el resultado y difundirlo con una aclaración sobre su carácter no oficial.
Cómo elegir las referencias visuales para la creación de la IA
El primer paso consiste en descargar imágenes de Los Saja Boys y de Tom y Jerry en alta calidad y que no tengan marcas de agua que afecten el trabajo de la IA.
PUBLICIDAD
Es clave que las imágenes integren carreras rápidas, expresiones de sorpresa, movimientos físicos exagerados, objetos que vuelan y accidentes domésticos permiten recuperar el ritmo de una persecución sin nombrar ni copiar a los personajes de una franquicia.
Qué plataforma es útil para generar imágenes con IA
Una vez elegidos los archivos, se pueden incorporar al chat de Gemini desde la opción de adjuntar imágenes. Las referencias sirven para orientar el resultado en aspectos como la iluminación, el ambiente, la paleta de colores, la posición de los protagonistas y el tipo de trazo.
PUBLICIDAD
La herramienta puede tomar esos elementos como una guía visual, aunque la descripción escrita define buena parte de la composición final. No se debe cargar únicamente material oficial de una película o una serie para solicitar una copia exacta.
Resulta más útil sumar referencias distintas y explicar qué se busca de cada una. Por ejemplo, una ilustración de un escenario musical puede aportar las luces y la distribución espacial, mientras que otra imagen puede ayudar a definir los gestos y el tono de humor.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo redactar el prompt para la generación de imágenes de la IA
El prompt debe explicar quiénes aparecen, qué sucede, dónde se desarrolla la acción y con qué recursos gráficos. Una primera versión puede ser: “Ilustración animada original de cuatro integrantes de una banda ficticia de pop coreano en un escenario retrofuturista. Un gato gris caricaturesco persigue a un ratón pequeño entre micrófonos, parlantes, cables y teclados”.
Luego se pueden añadir precisiones sobre el vestuario y la estética: “Los músicos llevan chaquetas escénicas oscuras, accesorios futuristas y expresiones de sorpresa. Trazos de animación tradicional, formas redondeadas, humor físico, objetos que vuelan, perspectiva inclinada y composición dinámica”.
PUBLICIDAD
De qué forma descargar la imagen y revisar detalles u errores
La primera generación permite detectar qué ajustes necesita la escena. Si los integrantes de la banda aparecen muy realistas, se puede pedir una segunda versión con “rasgos caricaturescos”, “proporciones simplificadas”, “líneas marcadas” y “expresiones faciales amplias”.
Si el gato y el ratón recuerdan mucho a figuras conocidas, corresponde cambiar el color del pelaje, las orejas, los ojos, el tamaño y los accesorios.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo publicar la ilustración hecha con IA en redes sociales
La difusión requiere una aclaración que identifique el origen de la pieza. Una leyenda posible es: “Ilustración generada con inteligencia artificial, no oficial e inspirada en recursos de animación y pop coreano”.
La frase evita que el público interprete que se trata de una imagen publicada o aprobada por las empresas vinculadas con las obras de referencia.
PUBLICIDAD
Asimismo, conviene evitar textos que presenten el contenido como una escena real de Las Guerreras K-pop o de Tom y Jerry. La publicación debe describirse como una creación original elaborada con inteligencia artificial.
El uso de plataformas legítimas, junto con la revisión de los archivos antes de subirlos, reduce riesgos vinculados con aplicaciones no verificadas, fallas de seguridad o contenidos ajenos a la propuesta inicial.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Samsung renova linha de TVs premium com Micro RGB, OLED e Neo QLED • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Samsung renova linha de TVs premium com Micro RGB, OLED e Neo QLED
Nova geração da linha Vision AI reúne telas de 48 a 85 polegadas, com preços entre R$ 4.749 e R$ 42.499.
A Samsung anunciou nesta segunda-feira (14/09) a chegada ao Brasil da nova geração de TVs da família Vision AI. O portfólio inclui a estreia nacional da tecnologia Micro RGB, além de novos modelos das linhas OLED, Neo QLED e The Frame Pro.
As TVs têm tamanhos entre 48 e 85 polegedas e incorporam recursos de IA para aprimoramento de imagem e som, além de trazer funções para interação por voz e controle de rotina. Os aparelhos já estão disponíveis em preços que chegam a R$ 42.499:
A principal novidade são as TVs com a tecnologia Micro RGB, em que, em vez da retroiluminação convencional com LEDs brancos, usa LEDs minúsculos capazes de emitir luz sem a necessidade de materiais orgânicos, como os painéis OLED.
Os painéis com a tecnologia chegam ao país nas TVs R85G e R95H. O modelo maior é o mesmo que a Samsung apresentou durante a CES 2026 com 130 polegadas, mas teremos por aqui uma versão menor, de 85 polegadas. A R85H traz mais opções de tamanho: 55, 65 e 75 polegadas.
O modelo R95H traz recursos como HDR10+ nos modos Adaptative, Gaming e Advanced, além do sistema Auto HDR Remastering Pro. A tela chega a 165 Hz e tem quatro entradas HDMI compatíveis com sinal 4K, enquanto o sistema de áudio inclui 4.2.2 canais com 70 W de potência e Dolby Atmos. O aparelho também conta com amplificação ativa de voz, áudio adaptativo e recurso de áudio imersivo em 360 graus.
A R85H utiliza a mesma tecnologia de painel, mas tem especificações um pouco mais simples. O modelo tem taxa de atualização máxima de 144 Hz e mantém as quatro portas HDMI com suporte a 4K. No áudio, porém, são dois canais com 30 W de potência, também com tecnologia Dolby Atmos.
Os dois modelos têm Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3, quatro HDMI, duas portas USB-A, Ethernet e eARC, além de suporte ao padrão Auracast.
A empresa também atualizou as linhas OLED, Neo QLED e The Frame Pro. Os modelos são:
As TVs premium da Samsung também recebem o pacote Vision AI, que concentra recursos de inteligência artificial para imagem, som e interação. Para o último caso, a Vision AI Companion é a principal novidade. O recurso combina os assistentes Bixby e Google Gemini para responder perguntas por voz e analisar o conteúdo na televisão.
Para áudio, a Samsung apresenta o Áudio em Camadas com IA, que identifica diferentes elementos da trilha sonora e permite separá-los. Em uma partida de futebol, por exemplo, a empresa afirma que o usuário pode priorizar a narração ou som ambiente do estádio.
Já o Imagem Aprimorada com IA faz o que o nome indica: ajusta características como nitidez, brilho e profundidade de acordo com a cena, enquanto o processamento tenta melhorar conteúdos de resolução inferior.
Há ainda funções como Live Translate, papel de parede gerado por IA, Modo Futebol AI e o Modo Cuidado com o Pet, que usa o microfone da TV para identificar sons de animais e reproduzir conteúdos destinados a acalmá-los quando os tutores estão fora.

articles.title: Salesforce deepens its integrations with AWS and Google Cloud to support AI agents - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Salesforce deepens its integrations with AWS and Google Cloud to support AI agents
Salesforce Inc. is stretching its data and artificial intelligence tentacles further into the public cloud, announcing expanded strategic integrations with both Amazon Web Services Inc. and Google Cloud.
The partnerships, announced at Dreamforce 2026 today in San Francisco, aim to break down enterprise data silos by bringing rich and valuable customer relationship management data, AI agents and workflows into its partners’ public cloud environments.
Salesforce’s work with AWS is focused on bringing AI agents into the place where enterprises get their day-to-day work done, while enabling broader model choices for users and enhanced voice capabilities. For instance, Salesforce business context and actions are being made available natively within AWS’ business-focused agent Amazon Quick via the Model Context Protocol. That means Amazon Quick will be able to access live CRM data from Salesforce and leverage it to perform autonomous work on behalf of sales and customer service teams.
In another move, Salesforce said a number of AWS’s frontier agents, beginning with the AWS DevOps Agent, are being integrated within Slack, its enterprise-focused messaging and collaboration tool. With AWS DevOps Agent in Slack, teams will be able to resolve infrastructure problems without having to leave that platform, the company said.
Meanwhile, Salesforce’s Agentforce platform is being given access to Amazon Bedrock’s library of foundation models, including those from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Nvidia Corp., meaning users have more choice about how to power their Agentforce agents. In addition, Salesforce said it’s extending its Data 360 Zero Copy integration to AWS Glue-managed Apache Iceberg tables and the Amazon Aurora database, which makes it easier to ground AI agents in enterprise data.
Finally, Salesforce is enhancing real-time support for Agentforce users by adding Agent2Agent bidirectional audio support with Amazon Connect Customer over Websockets.
AWS Vice President of Data and AI GTM Rahul Pathak said enterprises need to build on their own data, with the applications and infrastructure they’re already using, to get the most value out of their AI investments. “These new integrations with Salesforce give customers data access without migration, model choice at the right economics and AI agents where their people already work,” he said.
A unified infrastructure for AI agents
Salesforce doesn’t have any preferences when it comes to public cloud infrastructure, for it used the occasion to announce a number of similar integrations with Google Cloud. The goal here is to build a “unified AI stack,” the company said.
The integration will enable cross-platform agent reasoning and actions that run on shared infrastructure, with Salesforce workloads brought onto Google Cloud via Hyperforce, which is a framework for running the company’s software on public cloud platforms. Salesforce said Hyperforce on Google Cloud is already supporting live customer traffic, and expects broader customer migrations to take place in the fourth quarter.
“What changes here is the infrastructure underneath our customers, not the trust they’ve built with us,” said Salesforce President and Chief Trust and Infrastructure Officer Meir Amiel. “Hyperforce running natively on Google Cloud will extend the same security, compliance, and resilience standards we hold ourselves to. Enterprises will get Google Cloud’s flexibility without giving up an inch of the trust bar they expect from Salesforce.”
There’s also a big integration with Google’s Gemini Enterprise platform to look forward to. Salesforce said customers will be able to surface their CRM data and other capabilities directly within Gemini Enterprise, without needing to do any integration work.
Instead, Gemini takes advantage of Salesforce’s new headless architecture, which is also built on MCP and brings Salesforce capabilities to any AI model or agent. That means Gemini can now be used to perform tasks like sales pipeline health checks, account summaries, and case triage across sales, service, finance and advertising workflows.
The Gemini integration also sees Tableau’s data analytics and visualization capabilities brought into Gemini. That will help ensure that every response is grounded in Salesforce data, meaning more accuracy and relevance, Salesforce said. And going in the other direction, Gemini is being brought into Agentforce, so Salesforce customers will also be able to develop agents powered by Google’s flagship AI model.
Finally, Salesforce said it’s integrating its Commerce Cloud platform with the Universal Commerce Protocol. That will make it possible for shoppers to discover and purchase products from directly within Google Search or Gemini, with payments processed via Salesforce’s secure infrastructure.
Kevin Ichhpurani, president of the Global Partner Ecosystem at Google Cloud, reinforced the need for business context to succeed in AI. “By bringing Salesforce into Gemini Enterprise, customers can now build trusted agents that reason across their business context and securely take action,” he said. “And with Hyperforce on Google Cloud, customers gain greater choice in how they deploy Salesforce on our AI-optimized infrastructure.”

articles.title: Meta pode lançar óculos inteligentes sem câmera ainda em 2026
articles.text:
A Meta planeja lançar ainda no outono do Hemisfério Norte um novo modelo de óculos inteligentes sem câmera, de acordo com informações divulgadas pelo The Information. O dispositivo, desenvolvido internamente sob o codinome Luna, representaria mudança em relação aos atuais óculos inteligentes da empresa, que contam com câmeras para captura de imagens e vídeos.
Segundo o relatório, a decisão de retirar a câmera ocorre em meio ao aumento do escrutínio sobre os recursos de gravação presentes em óculos inteligentes. O The Information teria obtido as informações com pessoas familiarizadas com os planos da empresa.
Leia mais:
- Meta é processada por suposto uso de fotos públicas do Instagram para reconhecimento facial
- Instagram pago? Meta lança planos com links em posts e mais recursos de IA
- Robôs em data centers: Meta testa automação e gera debate sobre empregos
Óculos teriam seis microfones
- Apesar de não contar com câmera, o Luna teria seis microfones integrados;
- Segundo o The Information, o conjunto permitiria que o usuário conversasse com o chatbot de inteligência artificial (IA) da Meta e também com o Muse, agente de IA para consumidores lançado recentemente pela empresa;
- O dispositivo também teria um botão na lateral para ativar rapidamente a Meta AI. Os alto-falantes seriam semelhantes aos utilizados nos modelos atuais de óculos inteligentes da companhia;
- A ausência de câmera, portanto, não significaria o abandono das funções de IA. O projeto continuaria apostando na interação por voz com os serviços da Meta, mas sem o componente de captura de imagens presente em outros dispositivos da categoria.
Lançamento pode acontecer em outubro
A Meta poderia apresentar o Luna durante sua conferência anual Connect, prevista para os dias 23 e 24 de setembro. Segundo o The Information, a empresa teria como objetivo iniciar as entregas dos óculos em outubro. A Meta não se pronunciou a respeito.
Até o momento, detalhes, como preço, disponibilidade e outras especificações técnicas do Luna, não foram divulgados.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: The Download: AI doomers, whistleblowing agents, and de-aged livers
articles.text:
The Download: AI doomers, whistleblowing agents, and de-aged livers
Plus: Trump has called AI safety fears a “hoax” and rejected more safeguards.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The AI industry has taken a doomer turn. What now?
AI chiefs Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Demis Hassabis are suddenly all in agreement: the latest generation of LLMs aren’t safe and everyone needs to figure out what to do about it.
It’s easy to be cynical. With trillion-dollar IPOs in their sights, OpenAI and Anthropic need to reassure investors that they’re the grown-ups in the room while at the same time hinting at the power of the monsters they have created and intend to tame. Calling for a slowdown does both.
Still, the vibe at the top of these firms really does appear to have shifted. But what does a slowdown actually mean, and how much should we trust the companies calling for one?
Read the full story about what could come next.
—Will Douglas Heaven
This article is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
Roundtables: could AI really kill us all?
AI extinction fears have gone from a fringe idea to a serious concern among people working at the world’s leading AI labs. But how credible are those fears, and what should we make of the warnings?
Today, MIT Technology Review executive editor Niall Firth, senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and AI reporter Grace Huckins will unpack the debate in a subscriber-only Roundtable. They’ll look at where AI extinction fears come from, whether they hold any water and what we should do if they do.
Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.
AI agents blew the whistle on their cheating colleagues
A group of AI agents asked to solve a series of math problems split into rival factions—when some cheated, others tried to stop them.
That whistleblowing behavior, seen for the first time in a recent experiment run by Google DeepMind, could have implications for alignment researchers trying to keep swarms of autonomous AI agents in line.
The experiment offers a glimpse of how AI agents might police one another. But it also shows how quickly things can go off the rails when they’re left to interact on their own.
Find out what happens when AI agents start enforcing their own rules.
—Amit Katwala
Donated livers can be made biologically younger
Once an organ is removed from a donor’s body, the clock starts ticking. Surgeons usually flush it with a preservative solution, bag it and put it on ice, where it immediately starts to degrade. The team has a matter of hours to get it into a recipient’s body.
But there’s another option: machines that pump donated organs with nutrients and remove waste products, essentially giving them a chance to be back in a body. Now, scientists have found that livers kept on these systems seem to get younger, at least at a molecular level.
The finding could help explain why organs kept on these machines tend to do better after transplantation. It could also lead to new ways to test the health of donated organs and potentially repair ones that might otherwise be discarded.
Here’s what scientists discovered about making donated livers biologically younger.
—Jessica Hamzelou
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Trump has called AI safety fears a “hoax” and rejected more safeguards
He says stronger guardrails could undermine America’s AI advantage. (NBC)
+ Trump has united against AI doomerism with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. (Axios)
+ Anthropic’s co-founder says AI kill switches may need to be mandatory. (BBC)
+ Bill Gates says we’ve passed AI’s risk thresholds. (MIT Technology Review)
2 OpenAI contractors are reading people’s ChatGPT chats 
And you can bet the vast majority of its 900 million users haven’t got a clue. (404 Media)
+ LLMs could supercharge mass surveillance. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The US military has confirmed it has weapons in orbit
It’s the first time the Pentagon has disclosed this. (Ars Technica)
+ Officials have not disclosed what the weapons are. (BBC)
4 A new brain implant can translate speech and gestures at the same time
The system converts brain activity into words and avatar movements. (Nature)
+ It helps people with paralysis communicate more naturally. (New Scientist $)
+ Eventually, they could control robots or exoskeletons. (Economist $)
+ China has approved the first invasive BCI. (MIT Technology Review)
5 New York has seized a dozen celebrity deepfake websites
It's the biggest-ever legal action against harmful deepfake sites. (CNN)
+ Deepfakes have targeted at least 138 women MEPs. (Wired $)
6 US environmental regulators are scrapping limits on power plant emissions
The move could lead to dirtier power amid surging AI demand. (Verge)
+ Trump’s EPA says the rollback will save hundreds of billions. (Gizmodo)
+ New technology is changing nuclear power. (MIT Technology Review)
7 The EU plans to restrict social media and AI chatbots for kids
Under-15s would require parental supervision. (Politico)
+ The rules would also cover video platforms and games. (Reuters $)
8 Chinese researchers have mapped a path to the “last AI built by humans”
Their five-stage plan aims for genuine recursive self-improvement. (SCMP)
+ But it might take a while to get there. (MIT Technology Review)
9 The real AI economy is being built by ordinary people
Workers are using cheap AI to expand what they can do. (Rest of World)
10 Two strange new forms of ice could exist inside Uranus and Neptune
They could help explain the planets’  magnetic fields. (New Scientist $)
Quote of the day
“The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”
—President Trump proclaims in a social media post that he’s the only protection that the US needs from AI.
One more thing
How creativity became the reigning value of our time
—Bryan Gardiner
Americans don’t agree on much these days, but there remains at least one quintessentially modern value we can all still get behind: creativity. We teach it, measure it, envy it and endlessly worry about its death.
Given how much we obsess over it, creativity can feel like something that has always existed. But the concept is surprisingly young. The first known written use of the word didn’t occur until 1875, and before about 1950 there were “approximately zero” articles, books, or essays dealing explicitly with the subject.
In his book The Cult of Creativity, Samuel Franklin explores how creativity became an unimpeachable value and why tech leaders have embraced it so enthusiastically. I spoke to him about why we’re so fascinated by creativity, how Silicon Valley became the supposed epicenter of it, and how AI might reshape our relationship with it.
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google have been in talks on AI safety for weeks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s global policy chief, told reporters on Tuesday that the company has been working with rivals Anthropic and Google DeepMind on AI safety for weeks, as first reported by Bloomberg. Lehane is reportedly in Washington to work with U.S. lawmakers addressing catastrophic risks associated with AI.
The revelation comes in the wake of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay, published Saturday, which called for the industry to work together to slow the pace of frontier AI and avoid catastrophic risks. AI leaders across the industry, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Google’s Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, supported Amodei’s letter and call to action, with Altman saying that OpenAI would join Anthropic in embedding third-party evaluators into the company to monitor for safety.
On Tuesday, Lehane admitted that the three companies have been in talks for several weeks regarding AI safety. Some, including Altman, have noted that such talks could put the companies at risk of violating antitrust law if the coordination is found to suppress competition. Amodei’s essay proposed a narrow government waiver allowing such safety coordination, but Lehane reportedly said the firms don’t need one.
The news confirms earlier reporting and hints that the companies were working together. In an interview with Fortune late last week, Altman hinted that he had been in private discussions with other AI leaders. This week, The Information reported that the three companies have been working together to create a standards body for the AI industry — something Altman reportedly told staff would need to happen without the support of the U.S. government.
Hassabis called on the U.S. in July to establish a new standards body to act as an AI watchdog, with the power to screen the world’s most advanced models and coordinate industrywide slowdowns if dangers progressed.
President Trump, for his part, has dismissed safety concerns as a hoax and pushed back on the need for tighter regulations, saying any slowdown would give China a leg up in the race. His key AI advisor David Sacks — a longtime investor with a personal stake in much of the industry — echoed this, saying fears of existential risk from AI were overblown.
At the same Tuesday meeting, Lehane said that OpenAI supports a provision in the FRONTIER Act that would force top frontier labs to allow “independent verification organizations” into their companies to ensure models are developed safely.
TechCrunch has reached out to Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI for comment.

articles.title: The Boox Palma 3 gets stylus support and a sleek redesign
articles.text:
Nearly two years after the last update to Boox’s smartphone-sized black-and-white e-reader, the company announced the Palma 3 with a sleek redesign, new functionality, and a handful of other small updates that may justify its significant price bump depending on how you plan to use it. While the Palma 2 launched in 2024 for $279.99, the Palma 3 will be $339.99 and is expected to be “available soon.”
The Boox Palma 3 gets stylus support and a sleek redesign
The next version of Boox’s smartphone-sized e-reader ships with Android 16.
The most obvious upgrade for the Palma 3 is the hardware itself. It still features the same 6.13-inch, 300ppi E Ink Carta screen as its predecessor (which is now quite a few years old), but it’s wrapped in a new anodized aluminum frame with a paperlike fiberglass backplate. The Palma 3 looks like a significant upgrade to the Palma line, even if under the hood you’ll find more of the same. The pocketable e-reader is powered by a Qualcomm Q-6690 octa-core processor with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage expandable with a microSD card. It also includes a 3950mAh rechargeable battery, a 16-megapixel camera on the back, and a fingerprint reader in the power button.
The original Palma and the Palma 2 came with Android 11 and Android 13, respectively, but the new Palma 3 ships with Android 16, which is just one generation behind the latest version of the OS. That should help it feel like a more modern mobile device. And like the color screen Palma 2 Pro, the Palma 3 supports the Boox InkSense Plus active stylus so you can use the e-reader as a digital notepad with your preferred note-taking app. But it’s not included. The stylus is an optional upgrade that will add another $46 to the cost of the Palma 3, pushing it closer to the price of premium e-notes like the Remarkable Paper Pure.

articles.title: Toronto Tech Week announces dates for 2027 edition | BetaKit
articles.text:
Mark your calendars, Canadian tech: Toronto Tech Week (TTW) is officially returning for its third edition in 2027.
Canada’s largest grassroots tech event announced on Tuesday that its third annual conference will run from May 31 to June 4, 2027, in Toronto.
“We want to … make sure we’re building for the whole ecosystem, not just the loudest parts of it.”
TTW co-director and co-founder Mellonie Truong is stepping into the role of executive director, while fellow co-director and co-founder Julia Konefal is moving to a strategic advisory role, the organizers said. Golden Ventures general partner Ameet Shah and (BetaKit majority owner) Good Future co-founder Satish Kanwar will remain on the board.
“We want to keep growing the week, while also raising the bar on the experience, creating more high-impact moments, and making sure we’re building for the whole ecosystem, not just the loudest parts of it,” Truong told BetaKit in an email.
As in past years, BetaKit will kick off the week with its marquee opening event, BetaKit Most Ambitious: Town Hall, on May 31. This will coincide with the release of the 2027 BetaKit Most Ambitious issue—an annual publication highlighting Canadian innovators making bold bets.
The 2026 edition featured talks and panels from several notable Canadian tech leaders, including Waabi CEO Raquel Urtasun; former Research in Motion co-founder and chair of the Council of Canadian Innovators Jim Balsillie; Canada’s AI minister Evan Solomon; and honourees from the defence and dual-use section of BetaKit Most Ambitious.
The conference, backed by a volunteer-run, non-profit organization, launched in 2025 to fill a gap left when tech conference Collision moved to Vancouver under a new name. In its inaugural year, TTW welcomed more than 15,000 attendees to over 300 events across Toronto. This year, the organizers said attendance doubled, with more than 32,400 attendees at over 600 events.
RELATED: How Toronto Tech Week became Canada’s largest grassroots tech event
The decentralized format of TTW allows attendees to create their own niche events—from hackathons and fireside chats to founder brunches and investor cocktails—for free, as opposed to a traditional conference format where programming happens in one location.
Co-organizers said that the goal for the 2027 edition will be to maximize value and impact for attendees, particularly as it looks to pull in a more international audience. This summer, attendees came from more than 87 countries and 517 cities globally.
“I hope we’ve been able to do this city justice, and I hope we can continue doing that by getting more people, in person, in Toronto in 2027,” Truong told BetaKit.
The organizers are expected to announce more programming, information on how to host events, and event partners in the coming months.
BetaKit is a Toronto Tech Week media partner. Feature image courtesy Toronto Tech Week.

articles.title: AI models need more data about biology, and OpenAI is paying to create it
articles.text:
AI models need more data about biology, and OpenAI is paying to create it
The OpenAI Foundation is funding a new effort called Data for Public Health.
Last year Ruxandra Teslo, a policy analyst who focuses on clinical trials, posted an idea for supercharging medical AI systems: Use data from failed biotech companies.
By bidding at their bankruptcy proceedings, she proposed, it might be possible to obtain detailed regulatory filings, manufacturing strategies, and safety data—types of information usually considered trade secrets. She called these documents “biotech’s lost archive” and said they could be used to help train AIs that would act as powerful copilots in the often opaque drug approval process.
Today the OpenAI Foundation, the nonprofit parent of OpenAI, said it would fund her idea as part of a new effort it calls Public Data for Health, which aims to help artificial intelligence make big leaps in medicine by paying to create “high-quality scientific datasets.”
The basic idea is that AI isn’t going to be capable of making important breakthroughs in curing disease unless researchers can feed the models much more information than they have so far.
“Everyone is recognizing that data is the biggest bottleneck in successfully applying AI to biology,” says Morgan Levine, a former vice president for computation at Altos Labs, a longevity company.
In its initial round of data grants, the OpenAI Foundation also announced that it would give $40 million to a program to collect data about novel cancer vaccines at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, and support OpenAdmet, a group that runs competitions in which researchers try to predict drug effects.
Teslo’s idea for a biotech archive received $500,000 and will be pursued by 1Day Sooner, an advocacy group representing clinical trial volunteers, which she advises.
“We expect many remaining breakthroughs in preventing and curing disease to come from pairing the intelligence of new models with more observations of the world—in other words, more data,” the OpenAI Foundation said in a statement.
OpenAI started as a nonprofit, but leader Sam Altman restructured it to form a for-profit corporation that develops new models, launches products, and is now planning an initial public offering of stock that could value it at $1 trillion.
Because the foundation holds a 26% equity stake in OpenAI, it is now be on track to become the richest charitable organization on the planet, potentially sitting on $250 billion in stock value. (By comparison, the Gates Foundation and a trust associated with it held about $180 billion at the end of 2025.)
Making good use of that kind of money will not be easy. The foundation, based in San Francisco, is still hiring for many key roles and started ramping up its grantmaking only this year. Its largest single gift so far, of $100 million, was awarded in August to the Common Health Coalition, an organization that helps patients get access to drugs for hepatitis C.
OpenAI’s charitable efforts come even as apocalyptic fears have broken out about the possibility that runaway AI could wipe out all human life, possibly by launching a deadly bioweapon.
Those fears have been stoked by AI company insiders, some of whom say the chance of human extinction within the next decade is 10% or more. Last week, Altman and xAI founder Elon Musk both endorsed a call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” so that risk prevention can catch up.
Jacob Trefethen, an executive at the foundation, says it essentially operates separately from OpenAI but shares an official mission of ensuring that artificial intelligence “benefits all of humanity.”
“We’re starting grantmaking when we think the best way to achieve that mission is to make grants to external nonprofits, research institutions, and other third parties,” Trefethen said in an interview. He says the foundation hopes to give away $1 billion by the end of the year.
The $500,000 grant to 1Day Sooner will help the group prove it can obtain the data troves of bankrupt companies, says the organization’s president and cofounder, Josh Morrison. He thinks nonexclusive copies of company datasets could be acquired for only “a few tens of thousands of dollars” each.
His organization is currently in possession of three datasets, two of them donated by Lumen Bioscience, a biotech that previously used the Chapter 11 strategy to gain insights into another company’s drug development efforts.
Morrison says two other attempts to obtain drug company files this year proved unsuccessful, after 1Day Sooner’s bids were not accepted.
Bankruptcies could become what some are calling a “new land grab” for AI training. Last month, Google won a bid to take over the corporate data of the failed carrier Spirit Airlines, including 100 million emails. That led to objections from flight attendants and others who worried that private or proprietary data could be exposed.
The drug company files that 1Day Sooner is seeking are known as common technical documents. They typically contain the back-and-forth between companies and regulators, as well as detailed scientific and medical measurements, and essentially provide everything that is known about a drug.
According to Teslo, who is a writer for Works In Progress and a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Progress, a think tank in Washington, DC, a stockpile of such files could help turn an AI into a regulatory expert, which in her view could be one of the main ways AI helps speed cures to market.
“People say ‘We will invent AI, and AI will cure cancer,’ but that’s very removed from the messy reality and the regulatory process,” she says. “About 70% of the money and time in drug development is spent in clinical development—organizing the trials and testing the drug—but despite that, the process is basically a black box, especially for small biotech companies generating the innovations.”

articles.title: realme acaba de lanzar el teléfono perfecto para todos los fans de Harry Potter
articles.text:
Se acaba de celebrar el 25 aniversario de Harry Potter y la Piedra Filosofal. realme ha aprovechado este momento para lanzar al mercado una versión del realme 16 Pro que está lleno de detalles y que seguro harán las delicias de los más aficionados. Es la segunda colaboración de realme con una saga famosa, tras la que realizó con Juego de Tronos hace no mucho.
El realme 16 Pro Harry Potter Edition es el mismo teléfono que vimos hace unos meses, aunque su batería ahora llega hasta los 7.000 mAh, pero está personalizado con muchísimos detalles que lo relacionan con la llegada de Harry Potter a Hogwarts.
Por ejemplo, el packaging donde viene el teléfono recrea de una manera hiper realista el baúl que recibe Harry anunciándole que acudirá a la escuela de magia. Se trata de una edición limitada ya que sólo se venderán 5.000 unidades en todo el mundo.
Un teléfono premium en acabados
Cuando lo sacamos de la caja, llama mucho la atención el acabado marrón en piel que da un aspecto premium con un estampado Argyle inspirado en la escena del ajedrez mágico. Por detrás podemos ver los escudos de las casas de Hogwarts, colocado en la parte central del teléfono.
El módulo de cámaras del realme 16 Pro Harry Potter Edition resultará para muchos muy familiar, ya que recuerda a los brillantes ojos de Hedwig. Por otro lado, el marco central metálico completa el diseño con la inscripción “Welcome to Hogwarts”, grabada a láser.
Volviendo al baúl, el Pack de Bienvenida de Hogwarts también incluye un conjunto de artículos personalizados con elementos que acompañan a todo joven mago que llegada a la escuela, como la carta de aceptación de Hogwarts y el billete de tren.
El pack también incluye marcapáginas con los escudos de las casas de Hogwarts, postales de los personajes que recrean la llegada de Harry, Hermione y Ron a Hogwarts; una funda para el smartphone con el logotipo de Hogwarts en relieve y un pin para el teléfono.
El realme 16 Pro Harry Potter Edition está ya a la venta por un precio de 699 euros y lo puedes comprar tanto en El Corte Inglés como en MediaMarkt. Un precio visiblemente superior al modelo normal pero que quizá para los más fans de Harry Potter merezca la pena.

articles.title: The EOS R8 Mark II is Canon’s lightest full-frame camera with stabilization
articles.text:
Canon announced the second-generation of its EOS R8 with a new retro-inspired redesign and the addition of in-body stabilization. That feature was one of the most notable omissions from the original R8 that launched in 2023 as a smaller, cheaper, and more accessible alternative to the Canon R6 Mark II for photographers wanting a larger full-frame shooter. While the new EOS R8 Mark II is slightly heavier than its predecessor at 1.2 pounds thanks to the additional stabilization functionality, it’s lighter and cheaper than last year’s EOS R6 Mark III.
The EOS R8 Mark II is Canon’s lightest full-frame camera with stabilization
The 24.2-megapixel camera features a retro redesign inspired by Canon’s old film cameras.
The Canon EOS R8 Mark II is expected to be available sometime in late October for $1,899 for the body only, or $2,099 bundled with a Canon 24-50mm stabilized lens. That’s more expensive than the original R8 that launched at $1,499, but more accessible than the $2,799 EOS R6 Mark III thanks to some lower specs and omitted features.
Like its predecessor, the R8 Mark II features the same 24.2-megapixel full-frame CMOS sensor as the R6 Mark II, while the R6 Mark III got a bump to a 32.5-megapixel sensor. The new R8 Mark II still exclusively uses an electronic shutter instead of an additional mechanical one, with high-speed captures maxing out at 40fps again. To ensure you’re not too late to a critical moment, a pre-continuous shooting mode captures up to an additional 20 shots before you press the shutter button.
The new five-axis in-body stabilization offers up to 7.5 stops of shake correction that can be expanded by pairing the camera with a lens featuring its own stabilization. The R8 Mark II also features Canon’s Dual Pixel CMOS AF II system with what the company describes as “more tenacious tracking” than what the R8 offered. The autofocus system can also recognize animals, vehicles, and people, with the option to register up to 10 different people by their faces and rank their priority.
Video capabilities max out at 4K/60fps, but frame rates can be boosted to up to 180fps by dropping the resolution to 1080p. As Canon is targeting the R8 Mark II as a potential full-frame option for amateur photographers, the camera includes 16 different color filters, an easy to way to increase or decrease depth of blur that handles settings like f-stop and shutter speed automatically, and creative bracketing that takes three photos with different brightness and color tones.
Following other companies drawing inspiration from older film cameras for the design of new digital shooters, the R8 Mark II eschews the curves of the original R8 for a more boxy and angular body. Canon credits the nearly 40-year-old EOS 650 and its pentaprism housing on top as the inspiration for the R8 Mark II. Other hardware upgrades include a new multi-controller joystick above the camera’s screen, which makes it easier to select focal points, and its single SD card slot repositioned on the side of the camera so it’s still accessible when using a tripod. Canon will also sell a matching $99.99 accessory that extends the R8 Mark II’s grip, making it easier to hold when using larger lenses.
In October Canon is also releasing a free new Windows app called Dual Pixel 3D Converter that leverages additional info captured by Canon’s dual-pixel autofocus system to generate 3D imagery from the 2D photos the camera takes. You can use the app to create a 3D photo with a background you can move around, a 3D model with the background completely removed, or short 3D videos demonstrating an animated perspective adjustment of close-up subjects.

articles.title: Neagley is the Reacher spinoff that fans have been waiting for — but the new Prime Video series is breaking any boundaries
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Let's face it: the only reason we're tuning into Neagley is for the woman herself, especially as we've been missing her in Reacher season 4. Maria Sten delivers as she always has done, but everything else feels a bit... same-y.
Pros
- +Maria Sten as Neagley is as excellent as she is in Reacher
- +The added grit and vulnerability to her own backstory works
- +Cool cult storyline
- +Equally cool action scenes sustained throughout
- +Better constructed than Reacher season 4
Cons
- -It feels exactly like Reacher... especially as Reacher himself appears
- -Fans will possibly want more Reacher/Neagley screentime
- -You still need to suspend some belief to get into the swing of things
- -Is it really all that interesting? I'm not sure
Why you can trust TechRadar
With Reacher season 4 still streaming on Prime Video at the time of writing, fans are divided on whether its pivot to a political espionage plot has worked. But there is one detail that unites them: the show was better with Neagley (Maria Sten) in it.
After three seasons of dedicated service to Reacher (Alan Ritchson), Neagley is now a spinoff all her own. Taking on the lead role, she's working as a private investigator in Chicago, learning that a beloved friend from her past has been killed in a suspicious accident.
Obviously, Neagley is hell-bent on getting revenge and bringing the killer to justice, and "puts herself on a dangerous path to uncover a menacing evil," according to Amazon. Who does that remind you of?
We might have changed the surname in the title, but aside from Neagley's return, it all feels very like Reacher. From the look of each scene and the eight-episode storyline structure to how new supporting characters are introduced and utilized, everything is feeling very familiar.
It's also no secret that Reacher himself (Alan Ritchson) will make an appearance in Neagley, a cameo which, while likely to provide plenty of entertainment and action, blurs the lines between the two shows even further.
Sure, some elements of the new spinoff have been effective (more on that below), but when the opportunity arises to create an entirely original story that's adjacent to an existing, beloved IP... could the creative team behind Neagley not have been a little bit braver?
Neagley is still Reacher... just with a different focal point
Even though I know that a review of Neagley is something that Reacher fans will be looking for, this is one of the rare times in my job where I don't feel enthused to write... well, anything.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Why? As a reviewer, the most difficult movies or TV shows comment on are the ones that are forgettably fine. It's easy to lift something brilliant up and fun to trash something that you've hated — but if a project has nothing to say for itself, you're stuck.
This is where I think both Neagley and Reacher sit in the TV landscape. Both are designed to be intentionally dumb fun wrapped in the popular package of a crime drama, and therefore, they require very little of you as a viewer.
Credit where credit is due, though. Where Reacher season 4 has potentially tanked its own legacy by getting too entangled in its political tone shift, Neagley has kept things much more straightforward.
Its overarching storyline is much more akin to Reacher seasons 1-3, with a surprising connection to a little-known cult effectively tapping into our continued love affair with all things true crime. There's a healthy mix of CGI and real-life action scenes, all of which are incredibly cool and draw you into Neagley's ridiculously varied day-to-day.
However, our new supporting faces are sweet and ever-present, but they don't hold the same sidekick weight as Neagley herself did as Reacher's right-hand woman. In short, it's swings and roundabouts on a fairly inconsequential level.
At the same time, this is Maria Sten's love letter to fans
This brings me neatly to my main argument: it almost doesn't matter what Neagley as a show has got right or wrong, because we're only really showing up for Neagley herself.
For Maria Sten alone, Neagley is exactly the Reacher spinoff that fans have been waiting for. Search for anything Reacher related on social media and you'll quickly find fans pining for Neagley to return to the main series, or for the pair to finally give into their (questionable) underlying romantic chemistry and make things official.
Not only is Sten as impeccable as she was in the main series, but she understands exactly what both fans and the story need from her character. The exploration of Neagley's past and backstory is easily the most satisfying element of the new series, getting into the murky depths of why she is the way she is.
Through this lens, Neagley pulls no punches and leaves no stone unturned while reaching its hard to swallow conclusion. Even while she's recounting hidden trauma in the most vulnerable way possible, Neagley herself remains everything we want from the TV presence we've sorely missed.
Frankly, I credit anything and everything positive about the Reacher spinoff to Sten herself, and if Neagley gets commissioned for future seasons (which I think is highly likely), she'll be the one that makes them satisfying enough to keep watching.
If you're simply tuning in because you're upset that Reacher season 4 is ending on the same day, I'd probably advise that you rewatch seasons 1-3 instead. When it's good, it's golden, as they say... and we're still yet to beat that run.
All eight episodes of Neagley will be available to stream on Prime Video on September 16.

Jasmine is a Streaming Staff Writer for TechRadar, previously writing for outlets including Radio Times, Yahoo! and Stylist. She specialises in comfort TV shows and movies, ranging from Hallmark's latest tearjerker to Netflix's Virgin River. articles.title: Salesforce debuts Koa, a specialized model built to reason about CRM data - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Salesforce debuts Koa, a specialized model built to reason about CRM data
Salesforce Inc. said today at its annual user conference Dreamforce that it has partnered with Nvidia Corp. to train and release Koa, a specialized artificial intelligence model that’s custom built for reasoning about customer relationship management data.
Based on Nvidia’s Nemotron model architecture, Koa is designed specifically to help AI agents reason through complex, multistep workflows within Salesforce’s Agentforce platform, so they can perform specialized tasks across CRM data. It’s an example of an AI model that was post-trained on specialized data, but in a briefing, Salesforce Chief Platform and Engineering Officer Rohan Kumar insisted that it has not tapped any of the vast volumes of customer information stored within its CRM platform. Instead, the company used its customer data to build a massive synthetic dataset crafted out of almost 30 years’ worth of internal CRM deployment experiences.
By using synthetic data that simulates realistic enterprise workflows across 14 industries, including healthcare, finance and manufacturing, Salesforce avoided using any customer data at all, Kumar said. “There is so much knowledge that we’ve sort of gathered in building out the CRM over the last 27 years,” he explained. “And there is this talk around domain-specific models, which take the intelligence the model already has and you then post-train the model. Basically adding more information specific to a certain kind of job. That’s the genesis of Koa.”
According to Kumar, Salesforce combined supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning and a technique known as “group relative policy optimization” to teach Koa how to execute multistep tool calls with accuracy. The company went above and beyond to get the training right, and in its benchmark tests, the results suggest that those efforts really paid off, with Koa matching or exceeding the performance of multiple leading general-purpose models on CRM-based tasks with three times fewer errors.
Salesforce said Koa will be useful to enterprise customers that want to try and automate long, multistep processes that usually require human expertise, such as routing support cases, updating sales opportunities, qualifying sales leads and executing multisystem workflows. Because Salesforce hosts and runs Koa within its own trust boundaries within Agentforce via Nvidia’s open framework, customer data never leaves its controlled environment, ensuring it can perform inference safely, Kumar said.
In early pilots, customers highlighted Koa’s ability to streamline complex sales operations. “Accounting requires navigating tax rules, financial data, documents and the unique circumstances of every customer,” said Ryan Teeples, chief strategy officer at 1-800Accountant. “Koa gives our agents the reasoning to work through that complexity step by step and use the right tools along the way. That means we can extend more of our accountants’ expertise across every customer interaction and help people get to the right outcome faster.”
Koa still isn’t generally available yet. Instead, it’s currently being made available to select customers via an expanded pilot program within the Agentforce platform. General availability is slated for winter, Kumar said.
Customers will at least be able to access Nvidia’s Nemotron models via the Salesforce Missionforce platform, a secure cloud platform for high-security operations. The company said it’s integrating Nvidia’s full suite of Nemotron models within Missionforce Operations to provide customers in regulated sectors such as government with “mission-specific intelligence” that taps into their most sensitive data.
This means customers will be able to run the Nemotron models within air-gapped networks and private clouds and automate back-office workflows such as procurement and supply chain management on dedicated infrastructure that doesn’t expose sensitive information to the internet.
Salesforce said it’s going to roll out Nemotron models for Missionforce Operations in October.
